papers.title: RAKI: High-Order Alternative Finite Differences for General Relativistic Magnetohydrodynamics
papers.summary: Binary neutron star (BNS) and black hole--neutron star mergers are among the most important multimessenger sources. Observations of these events could provide valuable insights into several unresolved phenomena, ranging from the efficiency of magnetic field amplification during and after mergers to the formation of magnetars and jets. Understanding these phenomena requires accurate modelling of magnetic field evolution, which remains a challenge for state-of-the-art general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD) simulations. In this work, we present \texttt{RAKI} (Relativistic Astrophysics Code Implementation of the Alternative Finite Difference Approach for GRMHD), the first GRMHD code to simulate BNS mergers using high-order alternative finite-difference methods with adaptive-order WENO (AFD-WENO-AO) reconstruction and a fully non-staggered, node-centred vector-potential formulation. The code achieves up to ninth-order convergence in smooth test problems while accurately capturing discontinuities. In magnetised Tolman--Oppenheimer--Volkoff (TOV) star tests, \texttt{RAKI} retains $99.2$ per cent of the initial maximum magnetic field strength over ${\sim}2$ ms, exhibiting an order of magnitude less magnetic field loss than a reference GRMHD code at the same resolution. In BNS merger simulations, fifth-order AFD-WENO-AO reconstruction yields approximately third-order convergence of the gravitational-wave phase in both magnetised and unmagnetised models. The discrete no-monopole constraint is preserved to machine precision without staggered grids, even during BNS mergers with moving refinement regions. These results establish \texttt{RAKI} as a high-order, non-staggered GRMHD framework for accurate modelling of magnetic field evolution in neutron star mergers and its implications for multimessenger astrophysics.

papers.title: Dark-field Search for Quantum Vacuum Signals in the Low-Energy Regime
papers.summary: We report on the experimental details of a dark-field search for light-by-light scattering signals performed at the High Energy Density (HED) instrument of the European XFEL (EuXFEL) in a pump-probe type experiment colliding the EuXFEL beam with the 300-TW-class near-infrared Relativistic Laser at XFEL (ReLaX) at a center-of-mass photon energy of $\omega_\star = 116\,\mathrm{eV}$. Especially in combination with polarization filtering, the dark-field concept allows the signal-to-background ratio to be significantly enhanced and both polarization channels to be recorded. This work elaborates on the experimental setup and the diagnostics used, from the per-shot spatiotemporal-overlap diagnostics, via the polarizing beam splitter, to the characterization of the residual background. Moreover, it provides details on the start-to-end simulations of the setup used for analysis. Accumulating 2751 pump-probe collisions, no excess above background is observed, and an upper limit on the light-by-light scattering cross section of $7\times10^{4}$ times the QED prediction at a 95% confidence level is derived. This is the most stringent bound on low-energy light-by-light scattering achieved to date, representing an improvement by ten orders of magnitude upon previous experimental limits.

papers.title: Excitons in solid molecular hydrogen from quantum Monte Carlo
papers.summary: We use quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) methods to investigate the lowest neutral excitation of solid molecular hydrogen in phase-I under increasing compression, with emphasis on structural and response properties. We employ QMC wave functions for the excited state that feature only a single orbital substitution, or a multideterminant expansion including every single particle-hole transition, and compare the results with the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) and time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT). We examine a number of nuclear configurations representing thermal and quantum fluctuations. The effect of the multideterminant expansion is marginal on the QMC excitation energies but crucial on the exciton localization and related quantities, irrespective of full optimization and imaginary time projection. In the strong insulating regime at low density, multideterminant QMC results match and in some cases surpass the degree of localization afforded by BSE. A similar trend is observed for transition dipole moments and excitation-induced forces, with generally good agreement between QMC and BSE but marked discrepancies for nuclear configurations where localization differs significantly. TDDFT generally gives a more extended exciton with correspondingly weaker transition dipole moments. These differences decrease upon compression, as the system approaches a semiconducting regime where multiple particle-hole transitions are less important.

papers.title: Kelvin-Wave Multiplication by Sound Emission
papers.summary: A subsonic Kelvin quantum can emit a phonon and split into two softer quanta, increasing Kelvin population while losing energy. In the soft-phonon limit, rotational invariance relates the leading acoustic shear amplitude, odd under reversal of phonon axial momentum, to the energy released. Microscopic calculations support this dispersion dependence. In a reflecting cavity with coherent sound and Kelvin seeds, Gross--Pitaevskii evolution shows Kelvin gain, larger mean-square displacement and smaller mean-square slope; a $\pi$ shift of the initial sound phase reverses these changes.

papers.title: Benchmarking Quantum Neural Networks Developed for MBHB Coalescence in the Context of LISA Space Mission
papers.summary: Machine learning (ML) techniques are increasingly explored to analyse gravitational wave (GW) data expected from the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA). At the same time, advances in quantum computing have stimulated interest in quantum machine learning as a potential alternative to conventional approaches. We investigate the applicability of quantum, hybrid quantum-classical, and classical ML models to two tasks relevant for LISA observations of massive black hole binaries: GW signal detection and merger prediction. Using the Sangria dataset from the LISA Data Challenge, we benchmark several quantum architectures, including variational quantum classifiers (VQCs), post VQC hybrid models, quantum kernel methods, data reuploading classifiers, and quantum long short-term memory (QLSTM) networks, against classical support vector machines, multilayer perceptrons, recurrent neural networks, and LSTM networks. The models are trained on labelled data derived from the Sangria training dataset and evaluated on the corresponding blind dataset. For signal detection, several quantum models match or outperform classical baselines. In particular, the best performing hybrid post VQC architecture correctly identifies all signal samples in the blind dataset, while the standard VQC and data reuploading classifier achieve competitive detection rates. For merger detection and coalescence time estimation, however, the standard VQC emerges as the most reliable model, successfully localising all detected merger events with the lowest localisation errors. We further analyse the trade-offs between predictive performance, model complexity, and quantum circuit resources. Our results indicate that, although no universal quantum advantage is observed, selected quantum models can provide practical benefits for specific GW analysis tasks and represent promising candidates for future LISA data analysis pipelines.

papers.title: Non-Bloch Dynamical Quantum Phase Transitions with Memory
papers.summary: Dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) of periodic chains are determined by real Bloch momenta. We identify non-Bloch DQPTs, which occur only in open chains and are determined by complex momenta instead. They arise in a Hermitian chain coupled to a simple substrate, whose memory is treated exactly, and originate from the point-gap winding number $W$ of the projected propagator: for $W\neq0$, open boundaries change both the dynamical free energy and the critical times, even in the thermodynamic limit. We find that both follow from an analytic continuation to complex momenta, and show that $W$ can be measured by particle counting. This reveals a dynamical bulk-boundary correspondence, in which non-Hermitian topology emerges from Hermitian dynamics with memory.

papers.title: Static Response of the Strongly Coupled Electron Gas from Diffusion Monte Carlo
papers.summary: The local field factor $G(q)$ of the HEG describes how exchange and correlation modify the response to a static perturbation, and enters dielectric screening, effective electron--electron interactions, and the xc kernel of TDDFT. Accurate zero-temperature data for $G(q)$, however, remain limited to metallic densities, $r_s\leq10$. In this work, we present diffusion Monte Carlo calculations of the static density response function $\chi(q)$ and of $G(q)$ for $2\leq r_s\leq100$, and describe and discuss the methodological steps that enabled these calculations. We show how optimization of the perturbing potential in the trial wave function has an important effect, as a poor choice can reverse the sign of the response. A closed-form expression is provided for its optimal value, together with the density dependence of the linear-response window. We further show that backflow correlations leave $\chi(q)$ unchanged and that $G(q)$ depends only weakly on system size even at very low density, so that Slater--Jastrow wave functions and modest system sizes suffice. Together, these results provide a practical guide for future QMC calculations of response properties of the electron gas and real materials. Our results agree with previous DMC data at metallic densities for $q>k_F$, and extend them below $k_F$. They also agree with diagrammatic QMC at $r_s=2$. At lower densities, our results show that $G(q)$ develops a nonmonotonic structure at intermediate-$q$, where the response approaches that of the noninteracting gas. Quantitative agreement is seen with finite-temperature path integral Monte Carlo, suggesting that the previously reported finite-temperature structure is inherited from the ground state. Using a parametrization of $G(q)$ that reproduces our data throughout the liquid phase, we relate this structure to short-range order in the pair correlation function and the static structure factor.

papers.title: Single-atom billiards in an ultracold bath with energy-tunable collisions and threshold-sensitive detection
papers.summary: Transport processes at the microscopic scale can differ strongly from their macroscopic counterparts, particularly when the environment is not a well-defined surface but an unordered thermal medium. Ultracold quantum gases offer a high degree of controllability and directly observable dynamics, thereby providing a versatile platform to study such transport processes under precisely controllable conditions. Here, we realize an energy-tunable single-atom collider by transporting individual cesium atoms at controlled velocity through an ultracold rubidium bath. The constant lattice velocity sets the directed contribution to the collision-energy distribution, while the lattice depth provides a tunable energy threshold for collision-induced transport disruption. By independently varying these parameters together with bath density and temperature, we separate the number of collision events from their probability to disrupt transport. Across a regime with only a few expected collisions per passage, the inferred single-collision ejection probability rises from small values to near unity as the collision energy exceeds the lattice confinement scale. The experiment thus converts microscopic collisional energy transfer into a binary single-atom observable and provides a controlled link between individual scattering events and emergent dissipative transport.

papers.title: Adiabatic Variational Principle: Born-Oppenheimer Theory for Emergent Electronic-Order Dynamics
papers.summary: Recent advances in microscopic many-body methods have enabled increasingly accurate descriptions of equilibrium quantum states, yet large-scale simulations of emergent-order dynamics typically rely on phenomenological equations with prescribed free-energy functionals. We introduce the Adiabatic Variational Principle (AVP), a framework for deriving order-parameter dynamics directly from an interacting many-body Hamiltonian. When microscopic relaxation is fast compared with order-parameter evolution, the many-body state follows the collective configuration adiabatically, in analogy with the Born--Oppenheimer separation of electronic and nuclear motion. This assumption makes explicit the adiabatic closure implicit in conventional phase-field descriptions. Each instantaneous order-parameter configuration then defines a constrained quasi-stationary many-body state, and the Lagrange multipliers enforcing these constraints directly provide the thermodynamic forces driving the collective evolution. Nonlinear Mori--Zwanzig projection theory further connects the reversible dynamics to the microscopic algebra of the collective variables and relates dissipation and fluctuations to the eliminated degrees of freedom. Applications to charge- and spin-density-wave dynamics recover Allen--Cahn domain growth, resolve evolving domain networks together with their microscopic electronic structure, and yield generalized Landau--Lifshitz dynamics for itinerant magnetism. The AVP thus provides a solver-independent microscopic foundation for phase-field-like simulations of the nonequilibrium dynamics of emergent electronic order.

papers.title: Cubic-Zn(1-x)Mn(x)Te optical modes across the phonon and phonon-polariton regimes
papers.summary: Alloying offers a convenient route to tune the physical properties of semiconductors, at the price, however, of local lattice/bond distortions needed to accommodate the lattice mismatch. Being nearly lattice-matched and moreover highly resistant to lattice and bond distortions thanks to a largely covalent bonding, cubic Zn(1-x)Mn(x)Te sets a benchmark to test the sensitivity of lattice vibrations to minimum lattice and bond distortions induced by alloying. We explore experimentally the two transverse optical regimes of cubic Zn(1-x)Mn(x)Te (x<0.7), with ab initio calculations in support: (1) the phonon-polariton regime at quasi-infinite (photon-like) wavelengths averaging over the alloy disorder, probed by forward-Raman scattering, and (2) the purely-mechanical phonon regime down to minimum wavelengths nearly matching the lattice constant zooming into the alloy disorder, achieved by inelastic neutron scattering. The short Zn-Te bond is found to exhibit a compact optical duo distinguishing homo from hetero local bond environments (1 bond: 2 mode), as explained by the percolation model. This deviates from the historical Zn(1-x)Mn(x)Te MREI (modified-random-element-isodisplacement) scheme inspired from classical Raman and infrared studies, in which the optical modes are blind to the bond environment (1-bond: 1-mode). So, the test is positive, reinforcing the status of the percolation scheme as a robust decryptor of (even small) lattice distortions induced by alloying through the lattice dynamics.

papers.title: Beyond $\chi^2$: Ensemble null tests for reliable scientific discovery
papers.summary: Unrecognized systematic errors can survive standard checks and undermine scientific discoveries. Null tests and experimental controls can expose these failures, but averaging measurements or reducing them to scalar statistics can hide important structure. We propose ensemble null tests that compare multivariate distributions with references from observations or simulations. We demonstrate their benefits across science. In cosmic microwave background simulations, they detect systematic effects missed by conventional $\chi^2$ tests. In Gaia data, they detect velocity asymmetry as sensitively as an informed search. In a CRISPR screen, they expose a control mismatch in DNA damage and reveal which cellular profiles drive it. As scientific datasets grow, ensemble testing turns repeated measurements into a broader search for unknown unknowns, strengthening the empirical foundation for scientific discovery.

papers.title: When chaos meets thermodynamics: from Fermi acceleration to thermalisation
papers.summary: A particle colliding with a moving wall provides one of the simplest mechanical settings in which a small system can exchange energy with its surroundings. In a chaotic time-dependent billiard, repeated elastic impacts may produce Fermi acceleration, with the characteristic kinetic energy growing without bound. This result poses an instructive thermodynamic puzzle: a physical wall maintained at finite temperature should act as a reservoir and drive a dilute gas toward a stationary temperature rather than heat it indefinitely. We use this puzzle to connect nonlinear dynamics with elementary thermodynamics. Under suitable decorrelation assumptions, collision sequences generate effective diffusion in velocity space and the square-root growth associated with normal diffusion. We then introduce two ingredients absent from the conservative accelerator: phase randomisation, which simplifies the statistics of energy exchange, and dissipation, which transfers energy back to unresolved degrees of freedom of the boundary. Their competition replaces unbounded acceleration by a stationary kinetic-energy scale. A recurrence for the second velocity moment yields a stationary kinetic-temperature scale $T_\infty=(mA^2/8k_B)(1+\gamma)/(1-\gamma)$, where $A$ measures the boundary forcing and $\gamma$ is a restitution coefficient. We compare relaxation in collision number with a simple Fourier-inspired heat-transfer model in physical time, emphasising that the two clocks are not interchangeable during transients. The resulting picture shows how fluctuations, dissipation, coarse graining and relaxation can produce an effective thermal state from chaotic dynamics while also clarifying the limits of the thermodynamic analogy.

papers.title: posterior-landscape: morphological feature finding in two-dimensional probability densities
papers.summary: We present posterior-landscape, a Python framework to identify and characterize morphological features in two-dimensional probability densities. The framework combines concepts from topological data analysis, statistical density-ridge estimation, and scale-space image analysis. It extracts localized concentrations, valleys, ridges, and changes of slope; for Bayesian reconstructions, it propagates uncertainty in feature recovery, geometry, and correspondence across posteriors. The framework also connects two-dimensional structures to features in one-dimensional marginals, and quantifies their correlation with other inferred parameters. We validate the method on controlled densities, and demonstrate its use on gravitational-wave population reconstructions, where it provides a systematic way to identify and interpret population features and assess which ones carry information relevant for cosmology. The resulting catalogues also offer a common morphological representation for future comparisons between predictions and population reconstructions.

papers.title: Stationary Structures of the Boussinesq equations
papers.summary: We investigate the steady configurations supported by the inviscid two-dimensional Boussinesq equations in the periodic channel. We show steady laminar velocity fields (closed non-contractible fluid trajectories) coupled to non-decreasing density stratifications are necessarily stratified shear flows. The direction of density monotonicity along level sets is in fact fundamental: in striking contrast with the Euler equations, we exhibit laminar non-stagnant non-shear stationary solutions in the periodic channel. We also provide distinct flexibility and rigidity results (laminar persistence or appearance of islands for nearby non-shear solutions) close to stratified shear flows according to their stagnation points. As a by-product of our analysis, we establish a uniform Crandall-Rabinowitz bifurcation theorem that might be of independent interest.

papers.title: Electric field control of anisotropic spin traffic between spin-filtering and magnon-scattering in a layered antiferromagnet
papers.summary: Layered A-type antiferromagnetic (AFM) semiconductors offer a unique platform for spintronic devices by combining robust magnetism with gate-tunable semiconducting properties. We present a dual-gate field-effect transistor based on CrSBr, a layered A-type AFM with pronounced transport anisotropy and complex spin dynamics. Our device provides independent control over carrier density and displacement field. Systematic transport measurements reveal that the displacement field, rather than doping, predominantly governs the sign and magnitude of magnetoresistance ratio (MRR). We identify the origins of both negative and positive MRR components and connect them to interlayer and intralayer spin-dependent transport mechanisms. We interpret these findings with ab initio calculations and an effective spin-circuit model that reproduces the anisotropic magnetotransport. Our results identify the displacement field as an efficient electrical control parameter of spin transport in CrSBr and suggest that multi-gate architectures could provide similar control in other layered antiferromagnetic semiconductors.

papers.title: Time Reflection-Refraction Crossover at Topological Kramers Edge States
papers.summary: Time-reversal symmetry protects helical edge states against static nonmagnetic backscattering. We show that spatially uniform temporal modulation produces a time reflection-refraction crossover within the same quantum spin Hall phase while preserving time-reversal symmetry of the instantaneous Hamiltonian. A finite gap to the bulk and an edge splitting that vanishes at the Kramers crossing allow the modulation to suppress bulk excitation while remaining nonadiabatic between the edge channels. Virtual transitions through bulk states enable coherent conversion between counter-propagating edge channels at fixed crystal momentum. Near the crossing, $qT$ governs the leading crossover dynamics for a fixed ramp shape, where $q$ is the momentum offset and $T$ the ramp duration. Coherent interference can suppress and restore reflection as the ramp slows. In the adiabatic limit, two initially time-reversed wave packets follow their respective propagation branches and acquire equal geometric displacements. Their group-velocity contributions cancel, isolating the contribution from the Berry curvature to be directly observable. Temporal modulation thus controls protected states and quantum geometry along a topological edge.

papers.title: FCC-\mu e: High Energy, High Luminosity Muon-Electron Collider & Neutrino Factory at CERN
papers.summary: The concept is presented of making at the FCC-$ee$ (or CEPC) facility $\mu^+e^-$ collisions at the centre-of-mass energy between 1 and 2 TeV and the average luminosity above $10^{34}$cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$, concurrently to the $e^+e^-$ collisions. First, a concise scientific motivation is given, including the exciting prospect of measurements of the Higgs boson self-interaction, and is followed by a presentation of the FCC-$\mu e$ layout -- from the source of ultra-cold anti-muons, through the muon booster, to the main muon ring. Basic considerations are also given regarding the machine-detector interface and the performance of the FCC-$\mu e$ and associated neutrino factory. The paper concludes with an outlook underlying relevance of such anti-muon beams for any future high energy storage ring as well as for neutrino science.

papers.title: Static dipolar impurity in a Fermi gas
papers.summary: We consider a static dipolar impurity immersed in a Fermi gas and show how dipolar interactions shape both the few-body scattering properties and the resulting polaron physics. Using Fumi's theorem, we connect the anisotropic phase shifts directly to the ground-state energy, and compute the exact impurity spectrum via the functional determinant approach. The resulting spectrum is a convolution of independent even- and odd-wave contributions, giving rise to a ground state with simultaneously occupied even- and odd-wave bound states whose separation is tunable via the dipole length. A variational ansatz limited to one particle-hole excitation fails to capture this doubly occupied ground state. We further find that long-range dipolar interactions weaken Anderson's orthogonality catastrophe, reducing the power-law decay of the quasiparticle weight. These effects can be tested with ultracold polar molecules, where microwave shielding and independent tunability of interactions enable experimental access to the predicted regimes.

papers.title: Single-Temperature Ranked Greedy Cluster Exchange for Max-Cut on Two-Dimensional Tori
papers.summary: Ground-state search in two-dimensional Ising spin glasses on large toroidal lattices remains challenging for local-update heuristics because rugged energy barriers impede relaxation across metastable states. Equivalent to zero-field toroidal Max-Cut problems, these spin-glass instances also serve as standard benchmarks for optimization heuristics. Many Monte Carlo approaches combine single-spin flips or cluster moves with temperature ladders or annealing schedules, yet even with tuned parameters, rarely achieve rapid, reliable ground-state convergence at scale. Here, we address the need for faster ground-state search through cooperation between replicas. We introduce ranked greedy cluster exchange (RGCX) and combine it with fixed-temperature Metropolis sweeps to form single-temperature RGCX. Replicas are ranked by cut to determine the pair-processing order. Each pair deterministically exchanges every disagreement cluster that raises the better replica's cut, retaining the complement and conserving the pair's summed cut. On the 20,000-spin Gset instance G81, the estimated runtime to reach the certified optimum with 99% success probability (TTS99) was 12.1 s on an 8-core desktop computer. With the same population size, exchange interval and temperature, the method reached the best known cuts on all 17 toroidal Gset graphs, including 9 certified optima. These findings advance ground-state search on large two-dimensional tori by establishing single-temperature RGCX as an efficient population-based method that combines ranked greedy cluster exchange with fixed-temperature Metropolis dynamics.

papers.title: Grow, Compress, and Perturb: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Pathway to Scalable Quantum Chemistry on Quantum Computers
papers.summary: While Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) variants are among leading candidates for electronic structure calculations on quantum computers, gradient-based operator selection limits their scalability. To solve this, we introduce the Hamiltonian-gradient-free VULCAN (Variational Upbuilding, Layered Compression, Adaptive N-body perturbation) layered VQE framework. Our method dynamically generates ansatz operators using Variational Double Bracket Flow (VDBF) equations. Combined with a linearly scaling minimal complete pool, it creates a pool 4-12 times smaller than QEB (Qubit-Excitation-Based) pools. By appending entire layers simultaneously, Hamiltonian gradient measurements are completely eliminated. Circuit depth is managed via a grow-then-compress scheme using efficient state-overlap measurements, and qubit requirements are reduced by projecting the Hamiltonian onto a dominant-determinant subspace. Using high-performance emulation up to 32 logical qubits, we achieve chemical accuracy at just 5-20% of the measurement cost of batched ADAPT-VQE for hydrogen chains, BeH2 and H2O. For the 32-qubit C3H6, where batched ADAPT-VQE does not reach chemical accuracy, a single VULCAN layer combined with a GPU-accelerated stochastic Epstein-Nesbet (ENPT2) correction does. This stochastic ENPT2 post-processing step enables early termination at chemical accuracy.

papers.title: Odd Elasticity in Strain-Gradient Continua: Anisotropy Classification and Non-Hermitian Elastodynamics
papers.summary: Odd elasticity extends continuum mechanics to active nonconservative systems containing internal energy sources, such as robotic active metamaterials with nonreciprocal feedback. Modeling these systems as effective continua requires relaxing Maxwell-Betti reciprocity, which results in stiffness tensors lacking major symmetry. In this contribution, we extend this framework to 3D strain-gradient odd elasticity to incorporate the length scales inherent in these heterogeneous systems. By applying the full hierarchy of 3D point-group symmetries along chiral and achiral branches, we derive the exhaustive set of fourth-, fifth-, and sixth-order odd elastic stiffness tensors. Further, utilizing the dynamic principle of virtual work, we formulate the equilibrium equations, higher-order boundary conditions, and the generalized acoustic tensor for elastodynamic analysis. The results demonstrate that nonreciprocal moduli survive even under full isotropy in the sixth-order stiffness, under hemitropy in the fifth-order stiffness, and under cubic symmetry in fourth-order stiffness. In contrast, the elastodynamic analysis reveals that under isotropic and hemitropic limits, despite the underlying odd stiffness moduli, the acoustic tensor remains unconditionally Hermitian. Non-Hermitian elastodynamics is shown to require anisotropy. By numerically analyzing a transversely hemitropic odd elastic continuum, we demonstrate that this symmetry reduction results in non-Hermitian elastodynamic phenomena including exceptional points in the dispersion spectra and active energy exchange through simultaneous amplification and attenuation of the elastic wave components. These results provide the necessary theoretical foundation for future multiscale homogenization frameworks for anisotropic strain-gradient active microstructures, and for the design of nonreciprocal strain-gradient metamaterials.

papers.title: Exceptional Points as Witnesses of Non-Gaussian Noise
papers.summary: Efficient control of quantum devices requires the knowledge of their environmental noise, yet the commonly measured power spectrum does not fully characterize non-Gaussian fluctuations of realistic environments. Here we show that exceptional points (EPs) in the noise-averaged dephasing response can expose observable signatures of non-Gaussian statistics, distinguishing environments with identical lower-order statistics. We also introduce a theoretical model that describes dephasing environments in terms of identical independent noise sources while preserving the power spectrum. Given a calibrated single-source model, the largest EP order extracted from the measured dephasing response determines the number of sources and predicts the higher-order statistics of the combined noise. We illustrate an atomtronic readout that maps distinct EP signatures onto an evolving ensemble-averaged atomic interference pattern. Our results connect non-Hermitian dynamics to environmental noise statistics, providing a route to characterize noise in quantum devices used in computing, metrology, and precision measurement.

papers.title: Spontaneous Mutations from Terahertz Proton Tunneling
papers.summary: Protons in the bonds between base pairs of the double helix store the code of life by breaking the dyad symmetry that swaps the sense strand with its complementary partner. When these bonds break during replication and transcription, pairs of protons switch sides, restoring dyad symmetry and destroying genetic information. The observed rate of such spontaneous mutations is obtained in the sudden approximation for bond breaking provided protons in bonds between bases tunnel across the gap with terahertz frequency.

papers.title: Strain Functionals: A Complete and Symmetry-adapted Set of Descriptors to Characterize Atomistic Configurations
papers.summary: Extracting relevant information from atomistic simulations relies on a complete and accurate characterization of atomistic configurations. We present a framework for characterizing atomistic configurations in terms of a complete and symmetry-adapted basis, referred to as strain functionals. In this approach a Gaussian kernel is used to map discrete atomic quantities, such as number density, velocities, and forces, to continuous fields. The local atomic configurations are then characterized using nth order central moments of the local number density. The initial Cartesian moments are recast unitarily into a Solid Harmonic Polynomial basis using SO(3) decompositions. Rotationally invariant metrics, referred to as Strain Functional Descriptors (SFDs), are constructed from the terms in the SO(3) decomposition using Clebsch-Gordan coupling. A key distinction compared to related methods is that a minimal but complete set of descriptors is identified. These descriptors characterize the local geometries numerically in terms of shape, density, and orientation descriptors that recognize n-fold symmetry axes and net shapes such as trigonal, cubic, hexagonal, etc. They can easily distinguish between most different crystal symmetries using n = 4, identify defects (such as dislocations and stacking faults), measure local deformation, and can be used in conjunction with machine learning techniques for in situ analysis of finite temperature atomistic simulation data and quantification of defect dynamics.

papers.title: Lagrangian Stability Analysis Technique for Fluid Flows
papers.summary: Flow transition from a stable to unstable states and eventually to turbulence is a classical fluid mechanics phenomenon with a strong practical relevance. Conventional hydrodynamic stability deals with perturbation dynamics on a steady baseflow, typically in Eulerian reference frame. Common modal techniques, e.g., linear stability theory, involve linearization of governing flow equations and flow/geometrical simplifications, which can be tedious and restrictive. This paper presents a perturbation-free data-driven stability analysis technique by employing Lagrangian modal/non-modal analysis (Shinde & Gaitonde 2021), particularly the adjoint form of Lagrangian dynamics mode decomposition in the forward time direction. The proposed Lagrangian stability analysis technique (LagSAT) builds on the fact that a steady non-uniform fluid flow in the Eulerian reference frame can be perceived as an unsteady flow in the Lagrangian reference frame. LagSAT is demonstrated on classical baseflows that exhibit convective/absolute instabilities, namely, the self-similar Blasius/Falkner-Skan boundary layers, a 2D compressible flow past a cylinder, and a 2D compressible lid-driven cavity flow, producing neutral stability curves, N-factor estimate, and transient energy growth. LagSAT is naturally suitable for the global analysis of large/complex numerical/experimental baseflows with multiphysics effects.

papers.title: Light-sheet microscopy in cancer pathology: current applications, clinical challenges and future perspectives
papers.summary: Light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM) has emerged as a powerful research technology for three-dimensional (3D) visualization of biological tissues and is increasingly applied to human cancer specimens, including optically cleared biopsies and surgical resection samples. In this Perspective article, we review current applications of LSFM in oncology, and discuss how recent developments in microscopy, tissue preparation, labelling, and computational analysis are expanding the possibilities of 3D cancer pathology. Although LSFM has demonstrated the feasibility of large-volume imaging in selected human specimens, its application remains predominantly within research and translational settings and is not currently part of routine clinical pathology. We therefore distinguish demonstrated applications from potential future uses. We discuss how LSFM could eventually contribute to selected diagnostic and surgical workflows by providing 3D information on tumour architecture, spatial heterogeneity, metastatic dissemination, and surgical margins. These applications remain prospective and will require substantial technical, clinical, regulatory, computational, and workflow validation before clinical implementation can be considered. Ultimately, LSFM may complement rather than replace conventional histopathology by extending pathological assessment from two-dimensional tissue sections towards 3D spatial analysis.

papers.title: Quantum-inspired space-time PDE solver and dynamic mode decomposition
papers.summary: The numerical solution of time-dependent PDEs posed over the combined space-time domain, instead of treating time sequentially, leads to space-time methods. Treating time as another spatial dimension allows parallelization across time and simultaneous adaptivity in spatial and temporal discretizations. However, space-time formulations suffer from the curse of dimensionality due to the (d+1)-dimensional domain. Time-series forecasting methods, such as dynamic mode decomposition (DMD), also suffer the same scaling for storing and processing measurement data. In this work, we investigate whether quantum-inspired tensor network methods can mitigate this curse for both solving PDEs and data-driven modeling. We formulate a space-time matrix product state (MPS) encoding to represent either the space-time solution or time-series data. Using this representation, we develop a unified framework that combines an MPS space-time PDE solver with an MPS-DMD algorithm. We benchmark our MPS space-time solver for linear and nonlinear PDEs in both (1+1) and (2+1) dimensions, including non-diffusive regimes such as shockwave formation and Allen-Cahn phase separation. We observe that the MPS ansatz efficiently captures the spatio-temporal correlations of the solutions, with a 99% reduction in parameters with respect to the grid size. We demonstrate the MPS-DMD algorithm in two cases. First, the MPS space-time solver generates the MPS encoding of the time-series data. We then apply MPS-DMD directly to predict the dynamics without solving PDEs. Second, for the general case where data is available as dense arrays, MPS-DMD needs an intermediate compression step. We implement a streaming-like compression algorithm and observe a 97% reduction in memory, with MPS-DMD predictions matching those of exact DMD.

papers.title: Photon-starved imaging through turbulence at the diffraction limit
papers.summary: Atmospheric turbulence limits the resolution of ground-based imaging through rapidly evolving wavefront distortions. Fast acquisition can effectively freeze turbulence, but the restricted photon budget makes joint scene and wavefront recovery challenging. Here, we introduce Turbulence-Aware Poisson Blind Deconvolution (TAP-BD), which uses optical phase diversity to provide complementary measurements within a short acquisition window and increase wavefront information per detected photon. Poisson denoising and physics-informed optimization translate this information gain into joint recovery of the scene and a shared turbulence wavefront, with phase estimation errors approaching the Cramer--Rao lower bound in simulations. Experiments demonstrate reliable recovery from only a few tens of measurements under strong turbulence, with additional validation under severe photon scarcity. Simulations further show robustness to scintillation and temporal evolution over short acquisition windows. These results support photon-efficient imaging through turbulence, with potential applications in astronomy, remote sensing, and space situational awareness, particularly for time-sensitive observations.

papers.title: Phase-Space Shaping due to Betatron Cooling in Wakefield Accelerators and the Onset of the Ion-Channel Laser
papers.summary: Plasma-based accelerators are beginning to employ relativistic beams with unprecedented charge and ultrashort durations. These dense driver beams can drive wakes even in high-density plasmas ($\gtrsim10^{19}$ cm$^{-3}$), where betatron radiation becomes increasingly important and begins to affect the dynamics of the accelerated beam. We show that betatron cooling leads to a strong structuring of the phase space of the beam. This gives rise to bunched, ring-like structures with positive radial position and momentum gradients, \emph{i.e.}, population inversion of the amplitude of oscillation. We derive the characteristic timescales for this process analytically and confirm our predictions with multi-dimensional Particle-in-Cell simulations. The radiation-dominated regime of beam dynamics fundamentally alters the acceleration process and produces self-structured beams\reviewtwo{; Particle-in-Cell simulations of the resulting beams show that it becomes unstable to the ion-channel laser and lead to exponential amplification of radiation.

papers.title: Bubble curtains in a lock-exchange flow: the importance of transient dynamics in the curtain-driven regime
papers.summary: Bubble curtains are line bubble plumes that are used to mitigate saltwater intrusion in ship locks. When the lock gate that separates saline seawater from fresh river water is opened, a lock-exchange flow develops. Installing a bubble curtain at the gate location disrupts this flow and reduces saltwater infiltration. For real-world applications, it is important to quantify how effective the bubble curtain is as a function of the key governing parameters. To this end, we performed multiphase large-eddy simulations that faithfully reproduce earlier experimental results including the two distinct operating regimes: the breakthrough regime and the curtain-driven regime. This paper focuses on the curtain-driven regime and seeks to clarify how the effectiveness of bubble curtains evolves over time. The detailed spatial and temporal data from the simulations, together with the ability to systematically vary the governing parameters, enabled us to overcome several limitations inherent in previous experiments. Furthermore, the simulations were used to obtain parameter values to build a semi-analytical model. Both the simulations and the semi-analytical model successfully capture and elucidate the time evolution of the density field and of the bubble curtain's effectiveness. The findings highlight that the time elapsed since the gate opening and the transient dynamics play a crucial role in determining the performance of bubble curtains for mitigation of salt intrusion.

papers.title: Inertial rotation of a small oblate spheroid in a simple shear flow
papers.summary: We compare experiments and fully-resolved particle simulations designed to match the experimental conditions of a weakly inertial, neutrally buoyant, moderately oblate spheroid in shear flow under confinement. The study revisits an apparent discrepancy observed in earlier experiments, where a trajectory starting close to tumbling appeared to remain near the tumbling orbit, whereas weak-inertia theory predicts attraction to log-rolling for this particle shape. Experimental and numerical results are benchmarked against theory valid for asymptotically small particle Reynolds numbers and for unconfined systems. By accounting for confinement and inertia, together with sensitivity to initial conditions, and the finite observation time, we provide a consistent interpretation of the theoretical, experimental, and numerical results. Specifically, we show that log rolling is the only stable long-time orbit for the moderately oblate spheroid considered here; neither confinement nor finite inertia changes this orbit selection. Instead, inertia tends to accelerate the drift toward log rolling, whereas confinement reduces it, with the confinement effect being dominant in the present parameter range.

papers.title: The electrostatic-hydrodynamic interaction of two spheres in a linear compressional flow
papers.summary: We investigate the collision dynamics of two like-charged dielectric spheres in a uniaxial compressional flow, accounting for non-continuum lubrication interactions, van der Waals attraction, and the complete finite-dielectric electrostatic interaction. Mutual polarization causes the electrostatic force to behave substantially differently from the point-charge approximation and can produce strong near-field attraction despite far-field Coulomb repulsion, depending on the particle size and charge ratios. We identify a critical electrostatic strength above which particles approaching from the far field cannot reach contact. This threshold corresponds to a saddle-node bifurcation of the relative-trajectory field on the compressional axis. Below this threshold, near-field polarization-induced attraction can increase the upstream interception area and substantially enhance the collision efficiency. We report that electrostatic interactions lead to non-monotonic variations of collision efficiency with electrostatic strength, particle size ratio, and charge ratio. When electrostatic interactions remain repulsive at all separations, increasing their strength suppresses collisions monotonically. Non-continuum lubrication and van der Waals interactions further modify the collision efficiency, although sufficiently strong polarization-induced attraction can dominate these near-field effects. For weak electrostatic interactions, a perturbation analysis expresses the leading correction to the collision efficiency as a weighted average of the electrostatic force along the limiting colliding trajectory, with the weight concentrated in the lubrication region; this prediction agrees closely with the numerical results. These results demonstrate that finite-size polarization and near-field hydrodynamic interactions jointly govern the collision behaviour of like-charged particles in compressional flows.

papers.title: Performance Benchmarks for 2-View and 3-View Fiber-Projection Fine-Grained Particle Detectors
papers.summary: Fine-grained scintillator detectors are critical for precision measurements in nuclear and particle physics, where accurate reconstruction of interaction vertices and secondary particle directions enables separation of signal from background events. A well-known design choice is the fiber readout geometry: traditional 2-View systems use orthogonal X and Y fibers, while next-generation 3-View designs add a third Z-fiber layer that provides unambiguous 3D voxel identification. The 2-View approach suffers from combinatorial ''ghost hits'', which are false 3D candidates arising from fiber projection ambiguities, that degrade reconstruction performance in high-multiplicity events. This paper presents comprehensive simulation benchmarks quantifying the performance difference between 2-View and 3-View geometries across key metrics. We find that the 3-View geometry reduces ghost hits by 30 to 90% depending on event topology, provides robust vertex resolution across complex topologies, and maintains superior angular resolution for shower direction reconstruction. These benchmarks inform the design optimization of future detectors and provide quantitative guidance for reconstruction algorithm development across a broad range of experiments including neutrino physics, rare kaon/pion decays, and collider calorimetry.

papers.title: Precision Isotope-Shift Measurement of the ${}^1S_0 \leftrightarrow {}^3P_2$ Transition and a Multi-Transition King-Plot Consistency Test
papers.summary: We present precision spectroscopy and isotope shift measurement of the ${}^1S_0 \leftrightarrow {}^3P_2$ clock transition in neutral ytterbium ($\mathrm{Yb}$) atoms. By revealing a magic wavelength at $905.4(2)$ nm, we successfully achieve the atomic spectrum narrower than $100$ Hz. The interleaved clock operation between isotopes allows us to determine isotope shifts of four bosonic isotope pairs at Hz-level uncertainties, which is combined with those of other four ultra-narrow transitions in $\mathrm{Yb}$ and $\mathrm{Yb}^+$ to construct the King plot. We show that a rich dataset spanning multiple transitions enables a test of a restricted isotope-shift ansatz comprising the leading mass and field shifts, one effective factorized higher-order Standard Model contribution, and a new-particle contribution. Within this ansatz, the five-transition data are inconsistent with the new-particle contribution serving as the sole additional contribution over the mass ranges $m_\phi \leq 6.5$ keV and $18$ keV $\leq m_\phi < 100$ keV, while the previous works rely on another bound set by the neutron scattering and $(g-2)_e$ measurements. This work paves the way for the effective use of precision isotope shift data in the King plot analysis and stimulates further measurements in Yb and other elements.

papers.title: Decoding cell signaling via optimal transport and information theory
papers.summary: Cellular signal processing performs reliably despite molecular noise. Mutual information (MI) is widely used to quantify signaling fidelity, capturing how well outputs discriminate input states. However, it fails to capture whether the output preserves the statistical structure of the input, a property crucial in morphogen patterning and dose-dependent signaling. To address this gap, we introduce the 2-Wasserstein (2-WD) distance, which provides a geometric basis for comparing input and output distributions. We define MI as informational fidelity (INF) and the inverse of the 2-WD as geometric fidelity (GMF). Applying this dual-fidelity framework to canonical regulatory motifs under Gaussian channel approximation reveals topology-dependent trade-offs: coherent feed-forward loops can perform well in both dimensions, whereas feedback architectures reduce INF to enhance GMF. Experimental analysis of tumor necrosis factor signaling reveals dual-fidelity behavior qualitatively consistent with feedback regulation. RAS-MAPK data analysis further shows that jointly considering INF and GMF better characterizes intracellular signal relay than INF alone. Our results thus indicate that these signaling behaviors are not fully characterized by MI alone; instead, distributional correspondence provides a complementary dimension of signaling fidelity. Our study provides a practical framework for analyzing natural networks and guiding the design of task-specific synthetic circuits.

papers.title: Available Energy and Ground States of Convective Hydrodynamic and Hydromagnetic Instabilities
papers.summary: We propose a method for predicting the nonlinear saturation level of convective instabilities in neutral and magnetized fluids. The method combines Gardner's restacking algorithm, which computes the available energy and ground states of collisionless plasmas in phase space, and Lagrangian relaxation, where fluid elements find lower-energy equilibria while preserving local invariants. For the incompressible Rayleigh-Taylor instability, the problem is formally equivalent to Gardner's and the restacking algorithm directly applies in configuration space. To treat compressibility, we follow restacking with Lagrangian relaxation to obtain the ground state, and the results show excellent agreement with direct numerical simulations. Successful extension to the $m=0$ interchange instability in a Z-pinch demonstrates the method's potential as a general framework for estimating the nonlinear extent of convective instabilities, which can facilitate the design and operation of fusion reactors.

papers.title: Charge-Carrier transport simulations in diamond detectors with electric-field-dependent mobility and charge-collection-distance-based trapping
papers.summary: Diamond detectors are attractive for operation in harsh radiation environments because they combine radiation tolerance, fast signal formation, and low leakage current. Realistic detector-response simulations require an accurate description of charge-carrier mobility and trapping, which determine both signal amplitude and timing. In this work, we extend \allpix{}, a modular end-to-end detector simulation framework, with diamond-specific transport models. The implementation includes field-dependent mobility parameterizations for electrons and holes and an effective trapping model based on the charge collection distance (CCD), providing a detector-level interface to material quality and radiation-damage measurements. The mobility description is validated in the negligible-trapping limit using single-crystalline CVD diamond by comparing simulated drift velocities and transient-current signals with published reference data. For polycrystalline CVD diamond, the CCD-based trapping model is evaluated using experimentally measured CCD values and compared with laboratory transient-current-technique waveforms. The simulations reproduce the measured drift-velocity behavior in scCVD and the reduced charge collection and degraded transient response observed in pcCVD. The presented implementation enables detector-level studies of charge collection, pulse formation, and timing performance in diamond sensors using experimentally accessible transport and trapping parameters, and provides a practical framework for simulation-driven detector development and radiation-damage studies.

papers.title: Variational Framework for Quantum Molecular Reaction Dynamics
papers.summary: This work describes a geometric framework on molecular reaction dynamics based on the variational principle, where the Schr{\"o}dinger equation must be solved to ``see'' how a reaction occurs. First, the mathematical preliminaries are given by discussing the principle of least action and the mountain pass theorem. Second, we discuss the physical preliminaries, including the principle of equivalence for deriving the kinetic energy operator (KEO) and artificial intelligence (AI) techniques to build the potential energy surface (PES) in general spacetime. Moreover, we simplified electromagnetic interactions in curved spacetime within the molecular system and consequently, we are able to construct the nuclear Hamiltonian in nonzero curvature spacetime. This indicates possibility to introduce gauge fields through the curvature, such as additional term in the nuclear KEO near a conical intersection. Third, the single-particle approximation provides a powful ansatz to solve the Schr{\"o}dinger equation by variational principle. Thus, one can formulate the variational approaches for either electronic structure or quantum dynamics. In this work, based on previous discussions ({\it Phys. Chem. Chem. Phys.} {\bf 27} (2025), 20397) we unified them by a geometric description, where the geometric phase is naturally introduced. Finally, due to optimization characteristic of the present theory, further discussions on the present theory from optimization insight are also given, including two postulates, generative AI techniques, role of perturbation, and Markov process in optimization.

papers.title: Long-term scintillation light performance, calibrations, and triggering efficiency in the MicroBooNE detector
papers.summary: A detailed understanding of scintillation light in liquid argon time projection chambers (LArTPCs) is essential for the robust extraction of physics measurements from their data. This article presents the long-term performance of scintillation light production and detection using five years of data from the MicroBooNE LArTPC neutrino detector. We describe the MicroBooNE light simulation and light-based triggering schemes, and present the photomultiplier tube gain calibration and stability, light response stability, and light-based systematic uncertainties over the course of five years of data collection. We also make an in-situ measurement of the scintillation light triggering efficiency down to 30 MeV of visible energy. Finally, we discuss two notable observations in MicroBooNE's data, both reported here for the first time: an approximately 50\% decline in MicroBooNE's light yield over time, concentrated in the first two years of running; and a higher than expected O(200 kHz) rate of single photoelectrons (SPE). We present the first measurements of the dependence of the SPE rate on the TPC electric field strength and polarity. Together, the results presented in this article provide an important benchmark for the long-term performance of scintillation light systems in LArTPCs and their use in particle physics measurements.

papers.title: Role of anisotropic electronic friction in laser-driven hydrogen recombination on copper
papers.summary: Ultrafast light-driven chemical dynamics at surfaces are governed by energy transfer from excited electrons to vibrational degrees of freedom. When this nonadiabatic energy transfer is anisotropic, it can lead to dynamical steering effects that affect reaction probabilities or non-thermal final energy distributions in molecules. Here, enabled by a machine-learning-based simulation framework, we compare isotropic and anisotropic models of electronic friction during laser-driven hydrogen evolution on the (111) facet of copper. While anisotropic electronic friction determines the rate of energy transfer into the adsorbate and the fluence dependence of desorption probabilities, final translational, vibrational and rotational energy distributions are mainly governed by the potential energy landscape at the barrier and insensitive to nonadiabatic effects.

papers.title: Fast projections of two-dimensional light patterns using acousto-optical deflectors
papers.summary: Precise and flexible control of structured light fields is essential for applications ranging from optical trapping and quantum simulation to microscopy and materials processing. Acousto-optical deflectors (AODs) are widely used in these settings due to their high speed, large damage threshold, and ability to generate steerable optical tweezers. Multi-tone driving offers a powerful alternative to slow sequential scanning, enabling the projection of complex patterns with high accuracy as rapid acoustic modulation averages out inter-spot interference. In two dimensions, however, intermodulation between tones in orthogonal AODs can reintroduce coherent artifacts. We present a fast, feedback-free AOD projection scheme based on an incommensurately staggered frequency lattice that intrinsically suppresses such artifacts. For separable two-dimensional target patterns, our method removes the need for scanning entirely, enabling substantially faster and highly accurate projections. We further extend the approach to non-separable images using a minimal scanning strategy that maintains rather high projection speeds. These results demonstrate that appropriately engineered multi-tone AOD driving offers an efficient and robust route to high-speed, high-fidelity generation of arbitrary intensity patterns.

papers.title: A Reproducible Inertia Dynamometer for Vocational Schools: Design, Fabrication, and Pedagogy
papers.summary: We report the design, construction, and classroom use of an inertia dynamometer, built as a year-long project-based learning (PBL) activity with adult students at a Greek Evening Vocational High School (EPAL). The apparatus consists of a machined steel drum of calculated moment of inertia $I = 0.6507~\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, mounted on a student-welded frame and instrumented with a green-laser / light-dependent resistor (LDR) optical interrupter. The analogue output is sampled at 44.1\,kHz by the microphone input of a laptop computer, which is used as an opportunistic analogue-to-digital converter; torque and power curves are then reconstructed in software from the inter-pulse intervals via $\tau = I\alpha$ and $P = \tau\omega$. The drum's moment of inertia is cross-checked by an inclined-plane rolling experiment. A wide-open-throttle test with a 50\,cc scooter reproduces the expected flat-power / falling-torque signature of a continuously variable transmission in the low-to-moderate RPM range; the LDR's millisecond-scale recovery time imposes an upper bandwidth limit that provides an unplanned but pedagogically rich lesson in sensor physics. The project integrated industrial-lathe fabrication, arc welding, analogue electronics, and numerical differentiation into a single coherent workflow. We describe the apparatus, the physics, the signal-processing pipeline (for which MATLAB and Python/Octave code are provided as supplementary material), and reflect on the pedagogical outcomes for a student population traditionally disengaged from abstract physics.

papers.title: A hybrid framework integrating physics-informed neural operators with conventional methods for turbulence
papers.summary: We develop large-eddy simulation nets (LESnets), a hybrid framework that integrates physics-informed neural operators with conventional computational methods for accurate and efficient simulation of wall-bounded turbulence. LESnets incorporates the large-eddy simulation (LES) equations into the training of the factorized Fourier neural operator (F-FNO), requiring no labeled training data and accommodating flexible time horizons during training. Boundary conditions are enforced as hard constraints and a wall model based on the law of the wall is incorporated to improve physical consistency and enable reliable coarse-grid simulations at high Reynolds numbers. Furthermore, the immersed boundary method (IBM) is embedded in the physics-informed loss function to accommodate complex geometries with boundaries that are not aligned with the computational grid. In addition, the subgrid-scale (SGS) model coefficient is optimized during training using a single flow snapshot. The framework is evaluated on turbulent channel flows at friction Reynolds numbers $Re_{\tau} \approx 180$, $590$, $1000$, and $2000$ and turbulent flows over periodic hills at Reynolds numbers $Re_h \approx 5600$ and $10595$. Numerical results show that LESnets achieves predictive accuracy and computational efficiency comparable to those of the implicit U-Net enhanced Fourier neural operator (IUFNO) and F-FNO, while attaining accuracy comparable to that of conventional LES with greater computational efficiency. These results support the integration of physics-informed neural operators with established computational methods as a promising approach to accurate and efficient simulation of wall-bounded turbulence.

papers.title: Estimating the Kinetic Energy Spectrum from the Second-Order Velocity Structure Function using a Regularized Fitting Approach
papers.summary: Ocean turbulence plays a key role in shaping large-scale circulation, heat uptake, and biogeochemical processes. The kinetic energy (KE) wavenumber spectrum is a fundamental diagnostic, quantifying how KE is distributed across spatial scales. The second-order structure function -- computed from velocity differences between spatially separated observations -- provides a complementary measure, but unlike the KE spectrum, it reflects a non-local, weighted integral of KE over all scales. Analytic relationships link the two metrics, permitting forward and inverse transformations between them. However, recovering the KE spectrum from the structure function via the inverse relationship is highly sensitive to sampling limitations and numerical discretization errors. Here we propose a regularized approach in which the spectrum is assumed to consist of a finite number of segments with distinct slopes and amplitudes, and the inversion is formulated as an optimization problem. The approach is first validated in an idealized setting; for a number of idealized KE spectra with prescribed sets of spectral slopes and amplitudes, the corresponding structure functions are computed by numerically evaluating the forward relationship. These structure functions are then used to determine the underlying parameters using our proposed approach, which shows that we are able to perfectly recover the parameters and consequently the KE spectra. The method is further evaluated on high-resolution ocean model output, where it reconstructs the underlying spectra well even in the presence of noise. Finally, we apply the method to surface drifter observations (GLAD and LASER experiments). The results show that the framework enables estimation of the KE spectrum from sparse Lagrangian data, extending spectral diagnostics beyond gridded Eulerian measurements.

papers.title: Isotopic effect on collisional widths and shifts of Hg clock transition induced by cold Rb atoms
papers.summary: We study the isotopic dependence of collisional widths and shifts of the Hg clock transition $^1$S$_0$-$^3$P$_0$ perturbed by the Rb atoms in the temperature range from 1 nK to 1 K. For this purpose, we model the Born-Oppenheimer effective interaction potential by including the leading long-range van der Waals coefficients. For elastic collisions, we show the connection between the dependence of collision line shape parameters on the reduced mass of colliding partners as well as the variation of the scattering length in the excited and ground states of the Hg-Rb system in the $\upmu$K temperature range. We confront the full quantum scattering calculations with a semi-classical approximation for collisional widths and shifts. We show that the shape resonances in excited and ground scattering states lead to significant variations of collisional line shape parameters with the change of the reduced mass of colliding atoms. We also indicate the possible influence of inelastic collisions, which could lead to universal behavior and significantly affect the dependence of collisional broadening and shifting on the isotopic combination of colliding atoms.

papers.title: Squid funnels time their elastic recoil to amplify pulsed jets
papers.summary: Pulsed jets propel squid across nearly four orders of magnitude in body size. Each pulse leaves through the funnel, a soft nozzle, but whether its compliance acts within a pulse is not known. We tracked chromatophores on two squid species and found that the funnel dilates and recoils, with a repeatable phase lag, while the mantle is still contracting, and that the lag persists after denervation. For inertia-dominated jets, silicone nozzles, 3D fluid-structure simulations and a reduced-order model agree that the impulse reaches about 4$\times$ the rigid value when the nozzle response time is 0.2 to 0.4 of the jet-acceleration time, a range that overlaps the in vivo timing. The wall stores strain energy during acceleration and returns it during expulsion (akin to an elastic capacitor), which we term "superpropulsion". Synthetic nozzles tuned for superpropulsion launch jets farther in air, disperse dye faster, and drive a boat faster at a lower cost of transport.

papers.title: RPC Telescope Tests for Muon Detection at Laser-Plasma Accelerators
papers.summary: We report on a feasibility study conducted at the ELBA facility at ELI Beamlines in 2025 to investigate the possible production of muons from high-energy electron beams generated by extended laser-plasma interactions in optically generated plasma waveguides. Our team operated a portable, autonomous, and compact telescope based on Resistive Plate Chamber (RPC) detectors, positioned to detect high-penetration charged particles originating from the beam dump. The campaign demonstrated that RPC detectors can operate reliably and safely in the ELBA environment, even under intense radiation and electromagnetic conditions. The collected datasets, though statistically limited and affected by lack of beam control, allow detailed characterization of the background and validated the detectors' stability and tracking performance. These results confirm the feasibility of the approach and provide the foundation for a dedicated future run under optimized beam conditions, where muon detection sensitivity will be substantially improved.

papers.title: RadMaps: A Geospatial Framework for Simultaneously Modelling Capacity and Geographic Constraints on Radiotherapy Access
papers.summary: Access to radiotherapy is constrained by two compounding factors: insufficient machine capacity to meet patient demand and geographic distance from treatment facilities. Existing analyses address these factors separately, in turn constraining the insights available to advocates, planners and policymakers. This paper presents RadMaps, an open-source geospatial framework that simultaneously models capacity and geographic constraints on radiotherapy access at any spatial scale. RadMaps operates on Uber's H3 hexagonal grid and integrates population density data with GLOBOCAN 2024 annual cancer incidence estimates and the IAEA DIRAC facility inventory. Radiotherapy demand is estimated using cancer site-specific radiotherapy utilisation rates, and geographic access is modelled via configurable decay functions (step, exponential, Gaussian, or power law) of distance or driving time. A capped three-step floating catchment area (3SFCA) method allocates demand to facilities subject to both capacity and geographic constraints, producing a localised access metric for every H3 hexagon. Globally, RadMaps estimates that installed capacity could meet 68.5% of radiotherapy demand, and 73.0% of demand is within geographic reach of a facility (2 h driving time with Gaussian decay, H3 Resolution-5), both comparable with published estimates. When both constraints apply, only 60.0% is met, leaving 3.7 million patients per year untreated. Countries are also grouped into one of four access profiles: strong access, capacity constrained, geography constrained, and doubly constrained. RadMaps provides a flexible, open-source framework for analysing, visualising and identifying radiotherapy access gaps at regional to global scales, with applications in advocacy, infrastructure planning, and policy prioritisation. Its modular framework is also extensible to other spatial access modelling applications.

papers.title: Steelmakers increasingly cite scrap quality when closing material loops with their customers
papers.summary: The transition to a circular economy is pivotal for industrial decarbonization, particularly in the energy-intensive steel sector. While recycling scrap via electric arc furnaces offers a low-carbon alternative to primary production, the accumulation of contaminants in post-consumer steel threatens to render secondary material unusable for high-grade applications. This quality problem creates a market failure where traditional spot markets cannot guarantee the material provenance required for high quality (e.g. automotive-grade) steel. Here we show, using a massive longitudinal analysis of 1,163,561,858 news articles combined with global trade network data, that the industry addresses this partly through direct, vertically integrated alliances. We demonstrate that steelmakers are bypassing intermediaries to forge sovereign, closed-loop ties with manufacturers, effectively substituting market mechanisms with organizational integration. This reorganization coexists with a division between circular network cores in the Americas and Europe that pair their steel and scrap flows most tightly within their region, and economies whose steel and scrap flows are far less matched. At firm level, the quality of the returned scrap is a stated reason in twelve of thirty-six reciprocal loops closing after 2020 and in none of the eight loops detected before. Our results indicate that the circular economy is evolving into a geopolitical contest for material control, where competitive advantage is defined by the sovereign possession of closed material cycles rather than mere cost efficiency.

papers.title: Wind vector retrieval from miniaturized wave-enabled sea-surface drifters
papers.summary: Open-ocean in situ winds are sparse, limiting the calibration and validation of satellite wind products. We evaluate wind-vector retrieval from MELODI (Miniaturized Electronics Lagrangian Oceanographic DrIfter), a compact freely drifting GNSS/IMU wave buoy. Wind speed is inferred from the shape of the measured wave acceleration spectrum. A regularized regression with a gated nonlinear correction (Wind Inversion using Tikhonov Regularization, WITR), trained on scatterometer winds and evaluated by leave-one-buoy-out cross-validation against ASCAT MetOp-B/C and HY-2B/C, gives a root-mean-square difference (RMSD) of 0.91 m/s. Symbolic regression distills the trained model into compact spectrum-only and motion-enhanced equations suitable for onboard use; the reduced drag law gives 0.93-0.94 m/s. Wind direction is estimated, without any fitted reference-wind regression, from IMU-derived directional wave moments in the 0.60-0.90 Hz wind-sea band, with a circular mean absolute angular difference (MAAD) of 9.4 degrees against ASCAT. These differences are comparable to published scatterometer-moored-buoy comparisons and improve substantially on the traditional single-band Toba inversion. Validation is strongest from 4 to 14 m/s and sparse above approximately 16 m/s; stronger winds are assigned low confidence. The results show that small wave-sensing drifters, calibrated to the well-established scatterometer wind scale, can provide useful wind-vector observations for validating satellite wind products and for atmospheric and wave modeling; stronger-wind sampling remains a priority.

papers.title: Excursion-set structure factor of the auroral electric field
papers.summary: A spacecraft crossing the aurora cannot tell whether structures in the field-aligned currents are short-lived or merely small. However, by tracking clusters of coherent radar echoes from aurorae and Fourier-transforming motion-shifted echo pairs across radar snapshots, we can calculate the dynamic structure factor of the point-clouds, thereby quantifying the auroral electric field's spatial power and its persistence from 5 to 40 km, in regions where the radar look-direction is perpendicular to the geomagnetic field. This follows from the fact that coherent E-region radar echoes appear only where the ionospheric electric field exceeds the Farley-Buneman instability threshold, and so a point-target imaging radar naturally samples the field's excursion set; the field's spatiotemporal correlations are discernible from that point process. We find that the echo pattern moves with its cluster: large-scale structures persist for tens of seconds, but scales under 10 km renew within seconds, and conjunctions with Swarm satellite pairs replicate the same scale dependence in field-aligned currents. Coherent radar can thus quantify multi-scale variability in the auroral electric field on Alfv\'enic timescales.

papers.title: Collisionless dynamo seeds from phase mixing-induced electron slippage
papers.summary: Magnetic fields permeating the Universe on the largest astrophysical scales are thought to result from dynamo amplification in weakly collisional turbulence, but the origin of the seed fields remains an open problem of cosmic magnetogenesis. We identify a kinetic mechanism for magnetic-field generation in initially unmagnetized, collisionless plasmas, arising from phase-mixing-induced braking of spatially varying electron flows. Using analytical theory, fully kinetic Vlasov simulations, and turbulent scaling arguments, we show that this process generates coherent magnetic seed fields on scales far larger than the characteristic kinetic scales of the plasma, with strengths comparable to or exceeding classical Biermann battery estimates. The mechanism requires neither a finite initial magnetic field nor misaligned thermodynamic gradients and occurs naturally in electron-ion plasmas.

papers.title: No evidence of vorticity production from irrotational turbulent gravitational collapse yet
papers.summary: Gravitational collapse creates large amounts of kinetic energy that could potentially seed turbulence. If such turbulence were also suitable to initiate dynamo action, the resulting magnetic field would further modify the dynamics, especially on small length scales. However, a small-scale dynamo is believed to require vortical turbulence, whereas the collapse produces mainly irrotational motions, which may not be efficient for dynamo action. Here, we study the efficiency of vorticity production during a turbulent collapse. We adopt a barotropic equation of state, where pressure and density gradients are parallel, and no magnetic field, so that vorticity can only be produced by viscosity and by vortex dynamo-type amplification. Using direct numerical simulations of gravitational collapse, we show that, for the parameter space accessible to our numerical resolution, these effects are related to the initial irrotational turbulence and are not induced by the collapse. Vorticity production along with the associated small-scale dynamo action are still expected to occur for sufficiently large Reynolds numbers, especially when baroclinic effects are allowed for, but some of the earlier numerical evidence in the literature using a barotropic equation of state is now found to be the result of subgrid scale modeling and not reproduced in direct numerical simulations.

papers.title: Ultrafast All-Optical Polarization Control in a Plasmonic Metasurface by Selective Hot-Electron Heating of Orthogonal Gold Nanorods
papers.summary: Metamaterials tailor light's degrees of freedom through static designs, but sub-picosecond, all-optical control without sacrificing signal throughput remains challenging. Here, a metasurface is presented whose unit cell contains two independent, orthogonal and spectrally detuned Au nanorod resonators. A femtosecond pump polarized along either nanorod selectively heats its electrons, modulating one polarization channel while the other serves as an essentially unperturbed phase reference, turning a static wave retarder into an ultrafast, all-optically reconfigurable one. The transient response is computed by coupling a Three-Temperature Model, benchmarked against published experiments, with Finite-Difference Time-Domain simulations. Hot electrons damp and red-shift the pumped resonance, modulating the amplitude ratio and phase retardation of the two channels. In transmission at normal incidence and sub-mJ cm$^{-2}$ fluence, a 45$^\circ$ probe undergoes changes of $\approx$10$^\circ$ in ellipticity and $\approx$15$^\circ$ in optical rotation within $\approx$100 fs (relaxation time $\approx$4 ps), while its transmittance ($\approx$0.4) changes by at most $\approx$0.05. A second, delayed pump along the other nanorod raises these changes to $\approx$15$^\circ$ and $\approx$22$^\circ$ and, for a suitably polarized probe, cancels the intensity change of the first within $\approx$60 fs while the polarization stays changed. Selective all-optical control of independent resonators offers a practical route to transmissive ultrafast polarization control.
