papers.title: Design, Modeling, and Validation of Curvature-Based Shape-Aware Flexible Phased Arrays
papers.summary: In situ knowledge of array geometry enables mechanically flexible phased arrays to recover beam-steering performance under deformation without receiver-side RF feedback. This work presents a comprehensive engineering study of curvature-based shape sensing, combining numerical sampling-density and measurement-noise analysis, physical modeling of sensor response, and experimental shape and RF characterization. A study of 11,000 B\'ezier curves quantifies reconstruction error versus curvature-sampling density and noise, guiding the selection of nine sensing locations. A physical model relates PCB curvature to strain-gauge output voltage, with predictions compared against calibrated sensor measurements. The sensing system is integrated with an eight-element, 6-GHz flexible array and a low-cost, size-scalable, digitally controlled eight-channel phase-shifting module providing 360{\deg} tuning with better than 7-bit effective resolution. Across 12 fixture-conformed shapes, including five previously reported cases, the average reconstruction error is 0.06$\lambda$. Three additional air-suspended configurations, not prescribed by analytical curves, show an average positional difference of 0.095$\lambda$ between curvature-based and image-based estimates. Measured radiation patterns demonstrate broadside correction and steering to $\pm$30{\deg}. These results provide quantitative engineering guidance for designing and characterizing curvature-based shape-aware flexible phased arrays.

papers.title: Retaining Earth's Habitability Beyond the Life of the Sun
papers.summary: The Earth is rare and large-scale interstellar travel may be unfeasible - instead of migrating to other solar systems, future civilisations on Earth may have to remain. However, left unchecked, the Earth's current habitability will end in one billion years. This paper investigates and conceptualises a set of megaengineering concepts required to safeguard against seven long-term threats to Earth's habitability: solar luminosity, solar engulfment, the end of tectonics, water loss, obliquity and rotation, object collision, and extra-system threats. Implementing and maintaining the set of safeguards would allow the Earth to remain habitable for 9.1 quadrillion years. This could be raised to nonillions of years via capturing interloping interstellar medium onto Jupiter. Compared with alternatives, advantages of the safeguards such as greater feasibility, lower requisite rate of energy production, and utilisation of economically viable space mining infrastructure may present remaining on Earth as a more attractive long-term survival strategy.

papers.title: Comprehensive study of timing resolution in plastic scintillator detectors with wavelength-shifting fiber and silicon photomultiplier readout
papers.summary: We present a comprehensive study of the timing resolution achievable in plastic scintillator detectors read out through wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers coupled to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), combining a semi-analytical framework, toy Monte Carlo validation, and full Geant4 optical photon simulation. The analytical model traces the complete photon detection chain: scintillation emission, WLS fiber re-emission, optical transit time dispersion, SiPM single-photon time resolution, and electronics quantization. It expresses the timing resolution $\sigt$ as a function of the detected photoelectron yield $\Npe$, scintillator decay constants ($\taur$, $\taud$), WLS re-emission time ($\tauwls$), fiber numerical aperture, detector geometry, and readout electronics parameters. The analytical predictions are validated at two levels. First, toy Monte Carlo simulations ($2\times 10^5$ events per parameter point across 80 grid points spanning 8 fiber types and $\Npe$ from 5 to 200) achieve analytical-to-MC agreement of \add{$1.0000 \pm 0.0018$}. Second, full Geant4 optical photon simulations track the entire scintillation, wavelength-shifting, and fiber transport chain in realistic detector geometries, confirming the analytical timing predictions\add{ to within 10--20\% for $\Npe \gtrsim 10$} and providing first-principles photoelectron yield calibration. A comprehensive parameter scan covering 7 scintillator materials, 8 WLS fiber types, 5 SiPM models, 5 electronics configurations, 3 readout topologies, and 3 boundary conditions produces quantitative design maps and lookup tables for detector optimization.

papers.title: Photonuclear Neutron Production in OpenMC: Verification Against MCNPX, FLUKA, and a First-Collision Analytical Solution
papers.summary: The modelling of photonuclear reactions is increasingly important for applications involving high-energy photon fields, including accelerator-driven neutron sources, radiation shielding, medical physics, and fusion technologies. OpenMC photonuclear physics is currently available only in an unofficial development branch and requires independent verification before broader scientific use. This work verifies the OpenMC photonuclear implementation using six single-collision broomstick numerical benchmarks with 2H, 9Be, and 238U targets, irradiated by monoenergetic 5 MeV and 15 MeV photons and by a continuous 1-20 MeV LINAC-representative spectrum. OpenMC was compared with MCNPX under common ENDF7u photonuclear data, with FLUKA as an independent native-model reference, and with a first-collision analytical solution based on ENDF7u; calculations with the IAEA/PD-2019 library quantified nuclear-data sensitivity. Energy-resolved, angular, and integrated photoneutron yields were compared. Under common ENDF7u data, OpenMC and MCNPX agreed to within a few tenths of a percent in integrated yield, consistent with the statistical uncertainty, and their energy and angular distributions agreed closely, apart from small kinematic differences in the light-nuclide cases. Replacing ENDF7u with IAEA/PD-2019 produced deviations of up to 13.9%, largest for continuous-source 9Be and monoenergetic 2H (11.3%). FLUKA differed from OpenMC-ENDF7u by up to 9% (monoenergetic) and 2.5% (continuous source) and predicted a markedly different angular distribution for 2H. These results verify that the OpenMC photonuclear implementation reliably reproduces MCNPX under a given nuclear-data evaluation, while no single library or model is uniformly preferable from the present comparisons alone.

papers.title: Unravelling carbene moiety role in the N-heterocyclic carbene-phosphinidenes coordination chemistry: bonding and reactivity in gold chemistry
papers.summary: The coordination properties of the emerging class of N-heterocyclic carbene-phosphinidene (NHCP) ligands have been reported to be strongly affected by the carbene (NHC) moiety, but a clear understanding remains strikingly limited. In this work the bonding features and reactivity of 13 NHCP gold hydride complexes, [NHCPAuH], bearing different classes of NHCs have been systematically explored and compared to carbene analogues, using a consistent computational protocol. The analyses reveal that, although the $\pi$-acceptor ability trend of NHCPs qualitatively parallels that of NHCs, the $\sigma$-donor ability trend reverses, with more $\sigma$-donating NHC moieties generating less $\sigma$-donating NHCP ligands. Concurrently, the nature of the NHC moiety impacts the coordination geometry at the P center, with the CNHC-P-Au bond angle appearing as a structural descriptor to monitor and/or design NHCP ligands with desired $\sigma$-donor properties. The NHCPs stronger $\sigma$-donor and weaker $\pi$-acceptor abilities compared to NHCs and their unique structural flexibility and electronic adaptability have been showcased to be directly controlled by the carbene moiety via modulation of the HOMO lone pair energy and its atomic phosphorous 3p character. The reactivity of [NHCPAuH] complexes with CO2, taken as a probe for potential NHCP applications in small molecule activation processes, demonstrates qualitatively similar mechanisms, with remarkably different activation barriers, which directly correlate with the NHCPs $\sigma$-donor ability, thus reflecting the high tunability of their bonding properties. This work provides insights and perspectives on the design principle of NHCP ligands, with a spotlight on the pivotal role of NHC moiety in modulating their electronic and steric properties, offering opportunities for burgeoning applications across diverse fields.

papers.title: Transferable Fast Calorimeter Shower Generation via Multi-Geometry Pre-training
papers.summary: Detailed Geant4 simulation of calorimeter showers dominates the computing budget of high-energy physics experiments. Deep generative surrogates reduce this cost, but they have remained tied to the detector they were trained on, so each new geometry needs a large in-domain dataset. We study whether a single point cloud shower generator can be pre-trained on multiple detectors and transferred to unseen calorimeters. The pre-training geometries come from synthetic geometric variation rather than real-detector data. We introduce SimpleBox, a family of $10^4$ box calorimeters spanning the plane of sampling fraction and longitudinal segmentation, and benchmark it against pre-training on realistic detectors. On a calorimeter unseen in pre-training, with $10^3$ target showers for fine-tuning, the two priors reduce the aggregated sliced Wasserstein distance to Geant4 by factors of 5.2 (synthetic) and 8.0 (realistic) relative to training from scratch. At larger target sizes the synthetic prior performs better than the realistic one. Geometric diversity alone is therefore a practical way to pre-train a transferable shower generator.

papers.title: A swept-source dual-comb spectrometer on a chip
papers.summary: Dual-comb spectroscopy (DCS) enables high-speed, high-resolution spectroscopy by down-converting optical spectra to the radio-frequency (RF) domain through the interference of two mutually detuned frequency combs. Accurately resolving narrow molecular absorption features requires closely spaced comb lines generated by large laser cavities with long round-trip times, thereby hindering the miniaturization of high-resolution spectrometers. Here, we circumvent this limitation by demonstrating a swept-source dual-comb spectrometer using two unidirectional racetrack semiconductor lasers integrated on the same chip. The traveling-wave frequency combs are generated by strong RF injection at the laser cavity round-trip frequency of 14.3~GHz---otherwise known as quantum walk combs---and are continuously tuned in frequency by varying the laser drive currents. This enables continuous spectral sampling over a 32~cm$^{-1}$ range centered near 8~\textmu m, with an effective sampling interval of approximately 80~MHz. The outputs of both combs are coupled into the same monolithically integrated light coupler, providing automatic collinear alignment before the combined beam interrogates the sample. We benchmark the spectrometer against an external-cavity tunable laser and validate its performance using HITRAN simulations for 1.25\% nitrous oxide. Finally, the unidirectional comb architecture suppresses the detrimental effects of optical feedback, yielding comparable residuals even under deliberately introduced strong feedback. More broadly, the benefits of miniaturization extend beyond reduced footprint: chip-scale integration enables new forms of electrical and optical control that can fundamentally change how dual-comb spectrometers are operated.

papers.title: Constraints on redshift-evolving Hubble constant models with early- and late-time diagnostics
papers.summary: We systematically investigate four cosmological models within a parameterized framework that allows for a redshift dependence of \(H_0\): three phenomenological models (\(\alpha\Lambda\)CDM, \(\alpha w\)CDM, and \(\alpha w_0w_a\)CDM), and the $J$CDM model motivated by big bang quantum cosmology. Using cosmic microwave background (CMB) data, baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO), cosmic chronometer (CC) measurements of the Hubble parameter, and three Type Ia supernova samples (PantheonPlus, DESY5, and Union3), we perform Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analyses to obtain posterior distributions of the model parameters. We also perform separate analyses using early-time and late-time data to assess how each observational epoch affects the model constraints. For the three phenomenological models, the parameter \(\alpha\) describing the redshift evolution of \(H_0\) is consistent with zero within \(2\sigma\). The Hubble constant inferred from the \(\alpha\Lambda\)CDM model is consistent with CMB results, while the $J$CDM model yields a larger Hubble constant but is strongly disfavored by model comparison criteria. Using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) for model comparison, we find that the standard \(\Lambda\)CDM model remains the most favored by the data. Among the four models, the \(\alpha w_0w_a\)CDM model shows a marginal AIC advantage ($\rm \Delta AIC \sim$ -2 to -13). However, this preference does not translate into a reduction of the Hubble tension, which is consistent with existing studies supporting dynamical dark energy. Moreover, none of the models can simultaneously satisfy both the early- and late-time constraints, and the combined datasets alone are insufficient to conclusively determine whether these parametrizations can resolve the tension.

papers.title: Third-Order Algebraic Diagrammatic Construction Renormalized by Particle-Particle Ladders
papers.summary: The algebraic diagrammatic construction (ADC) of the electronic self-energy is based on M{\o}ller--Plesset perturbation theory. Its vertices contain bare energy denominators that do not capture renormalization of Hartree--Fock excitations through excited-state correlations. As we show here, replacing the M{\o}ller--Plesset amplitudes by amplitudes obtained from Epstein--Nesbet (EN) partitioning of the electronic Hamiltonian overcomes this deficiency at no extra cost by introducing dressed denominators that resum to infinite order the diagonal elements of ladder diagrams described by the pair propagator in the particle-particle $T$-matrix approximation. Third-order ADC with EN-dressed denominators leads to an almost fourfold increase in accuracy compared to standard ADC(3) on a challenging benchmark set for ionization potentials of closed-shell molecules, reaching an accuracy between that of equation-of-motion coupled cluster with singles and doubles (EOM-CCSD) and with singles, doubles, and triples. For open-shell systems, EN-ADC(3) halves the error of ADC(3) for weakly spin-contaminated molecules, outperforming EOM-CCSD, and still improves on ADC(3) for strongly spin-contaminated ones, for which EOM-CCSD remains more accurate.

papers.title: Direct laser-written optomechanical double membranes in an optical microcavity
papers.summary: Optomechanical membrane-in-the-middle systems that comprise several coupled compliant membranes offer enhanced optomechanical coupling and collective dynamics. Recent realizations were fundamentally restricted to two membranes and to limited structural optimization of the involved membranes due to their intricate fabrication and experimental integration. Here, we present a fiber-based Fabry-Perot microcavity incorporating monolithically integrated double-membrane resonators fabricated by 3D direct laser writing. We realize controllable mechanical mode hybridization of membranes with coupling rates of up to $J_{\mathrm{mech}}/2\pi = 0.16$ MHz, exceeding the mechanical linewidths. We demonstrate enhanced collective optomechanical coupling of the membrane stack's breathing mode, reaching collective coupling strengths of up to $g_{\mathrm{col}}^{(-)}/2\pi \approx 0.1$ MHz. Our transfer-matrix calculations predict further substantial enhancements with realistic reductions of membrane thickness and spacing, and a larger number of membranes. Our results establish direct laser-written membrane arrays as a scalable platform for multimode cavity optomechanics, combining tunable mechanical interactions, enhanced collective optomechanical coupling, and scalability towards larger mechanically coupled resonator systems.

papers.title: Signature of Short-Range Order in Static Response of the Three-Dimensional Electron Gas
papers.summary: The three-dimensional electron gas is a fundamental model in condensed matter physics and quantum chemistry, and the exchange-correlation energy derived from it serves as the starting point of \textit{ab initio} computations of materials. However, the wave-vector-dependent response, and hence the static local field factor $G(q)$, has remained without accurate ground-state benchmark in the strongly coupled regime for three decades. Using diffusion Monte Carlo, we calculate the static density-density response function and $G(q)$ across the liquid phase and find a pronounced structure in $G(q)$ at intermediate wave vectors, already visible at metallic densities and growing with increasing interaction strength. We identify it as a fingerprint of short-range order by showing that it is required to reproduce the static structure factor. Our parametrization, valid in the entire liquid phase, predicts a low-energy resonant mode inside the particle-hole continuum.

papers.title: Cascade models of anisotropic turbulence in magnetized plasma of solar wind
papers.summary: The solar wind plasma is modeled as a collection of discrete domains, each possessing local rotational symmetry about its domain-mean magnetic field. Based on this partial symmetry, we construct cascade models governed by the nonlinear and Alfv\'enic time scales. We introduce a stochastic renewal process with a bimodal waiting-time distribution determined by these two time scales. This process yields a two-branch renormalization solution for the total energy: a statistically robust branch with an Iroshnikov-Kraichnan-like $k^{-3/2}$ spectrum and a statistically marginal branch with a Kolmogorov-like $k^{-5/3}$ spectrum. Whenever energy-flux fluctuations become supercritical, the system selects the faster of the two available cascade rates, thereby preventing flux accumulation. During solar wind expansion, the system undergoes a dynamical first-order phase transition from the slow $k^{-3/2}$ cascade to the fast $k^{-5/3}$ cascade, with switchbacks accelerating the transition. The mixing of subcritical and supercritical domains in raw spacecraft measurements produces an apparent decoupling of the velocity and magnetic-field spectral indices. Incorporating a magnetic helicity cascade slaved to the energy cascade, we show that the large-scale spectra decouple into $k^{-3/4}$ magnetic and $k^{-3/2}$ kinetic spectra. For switchbacks inside the upper solar corona, the corresponding large-scale spectra instead decouple into $k^{-2/3}$ magnetic and $k^{-5/3}$ kinetic spectra. Data from Voyager, Ulysses, Helios, Wind, and PSP confirm the spectral signatures across heliospheric regions spanning heliocentric distances from 0.056 to 140 AU.

papers.title: A common warming-dependent decline emerges from divergent projections of tropical cyclone frequency
papers.summary: How global tropical cyclone frequency will respond to climate warming remains uncertain, with projections spanning both increases and decreases. Here we use an environment-dependent probabilistic tropical cyclone model driven by 14 CMIP6 models under intermediate- and high-emissions scenarios to identify a common response across these divergent projections. Initially weak global changes evolve into a clearer late-century decline, driven by increasingly negative changes in the Southern Hemisphere and diminishing positive changes in the Northern Hemisphere. The long-term decline is stronger under higher emissions. Counterfactual decomposition shows that this stronger decline cannot be explained by the sum of the individual predictor contributions, which largely offset one another, but is instead dominated by negative non-additive joint effects among absolute vorticity, vertical wind shear, relative humidity and potential intensity. Across 28 model-scenario projections, the global tropical cyclone frequency trend scales linearly with the level of global warming. Applying the fitted warming-frequency relationship at 2 degree C of warming relative to 1980-2014 narrows the 95% confidence interval for the projected frequency change from [-21.9%, +10.3%] to [-9.1%, -2.5%]. These results reconcile divergent projections through a common warming-dependent decline and identify the joint reorganization of large-scale environmental conditions as its primary driver.

papers.title: A Conservative Multi-Level Adaptive Velocity-Space Method for the Discrete Unified Gas-Kinetic Scheme
papers.summary: Multiscale gas flows often span a wide range of Knudsen numbers, from near-continuum to highly rarefied and strongly nonequilibrium conditions. Such flows require kinetic solvers that remain accurate across these regimes. The discrete unified gas-kinetic scheme (DUGKS) provides a unified description, but its computational cost and memory consumption are dominated by the size of the discrete velocity space. To alleviate this bottleneck, this work develops the multi-level velocity-space adaptive discrete unified gas-kinetic scheme (MLVS-DUGKS), reducing velocity-space redundancy while preserving accuracy and conservation. The method identifies the velocity-space requirements of individual physical cells from their distribution functions and groups these requirements into a small number of shared representative velocity spaces. This organization retains sensitivity to different local flow states without constructing an independent velocity space for every physical cell. A linear moment-constrained correction is incorporated to maintain discrete compatibility and conservative data transfer between representative spaces. Benchmark simulations spanning near-continuum to highly rarefied regimes show close agreement with the uniform-velocity-space DUGKS (UVS-DUGKS). For the cylinder and two-cavity problems, the average number of discrete velocity points is reduced by approximately one order of magnitude, yielding speedups of $7.00$--$7.93$ and GPU-memory reductions by factors of $6.73$--$7.49$. As a result, the MLVS-DUGKS provides an efficient tool for the simulation of multiscale nonequilibrium gas flows.

papers.title: Transparent 3D-printed flow cells for porous media studies with proof-of-concept on two-phase flow-reversal asymmetry
papers.summary: Porous media experiments commonly rely on geometry-controlled and optically transparent experimental flow cells. Examples include studies of flow structure, solute mixing, multiphase flow, bacterial dynamics, and reactive transport. Here, we provide a reproducible and open-source protocol to fabricate transparent monolithic porous flow cells by stereolithography 3D printing. The protocol covers digital design, resin printing, internal flushing, and resin coating. The flushing and coating steps are central to the workflow, enabling enclosed single-material cells to be cleared of uncured resin and made optically transparent for direct imaging. The protocol produces optically transparent, millimetre-scale, and quasi-two-dimensional flow cells suitable for simultaneous pressure and image-based measurements. As a proof of concept, we study flow-reversal asymmetry in steady oil-air two-phase flow in quasi-two-dimensional Hele-Shaw cells containing either triangular or cylindrical obstacles. Directional differences are quantified from pressure measurements and from image-based active-width measurements. The triangular geometry produces a clear directional response, whereas the cylindrical geometry remains symmetric within experimental uncertainty. These results demonstrate that our fabrication protocol can link digitally designed pore geometries to macroscopic pressure response and steady-state two-phase flow organisation. By making the design files, scripts, and manufacturing workflow openly available, we aim to make 3D-printed flow cells readily adaptable to other experimental systems and research fields.

papers.title: Damping by design in a bilateral electromechanical transducer
papers.summary: In a bilateral electromechanical transducer, energy exchange across the electromechanical interface allows the electrical termination to modify the mechanical response through electromagnetic feedback. The paper develops this idea from a simple magnetic pendulum, describing the electromechanical coupling through the flux linkage as a function of rotation angle. Torque and back electromotive force then follow from the same coupling function, making the bilateral nature of the energy conversion explicit. A radial-field moving-coil system provides a particularly simple realization in which the coupling becomes independent of angular position and the resulting electromagnetic damping is controlled by the electrical termination. A two-port representation then identifies this damping as an impedance-reflection effect and provides a quantitative criterion for separating the electrical and mechanical time scales. A numerical example compares ideal current drive with critical electrical termination and confirms the reduced second-order description against the full third-order dynamics. The resulting treatment provides a systematic and physically transparent route from familiar undergraduate electromagnetism and oscillator dynamics to electromechanical feedback, bilateral transduction, and the effect of loading in coupled physical systems.

papers.title: Thermal fluctuations and electronic readout using a moving-coil movement
papers.summary: The moving-coil meter provides a simple context in which to model deterministic electromechanical dynamics, thermal fluctuations, and electronic readout. The movement is a linear electromechanical system in which electrical resistance and intrinsic mechanical damping act as two independent dissipative channels, each accompanied by thermal fluctuations. The stored energy provides a Lyapunov function for stability, and the algebraic Lyapunov equation yields the stationary covariance in closed form. The result exhibits equipartition among the energy terms; damping is shown to reshape the temporal memory of the fluctuations without changing their steady-state variance, giving a thermal floor of a few picoamperes for a representative movement. Exact stochastic integration reproduces the stationary covariance and autocorrelation structure; the covariance is also recovered by spectral integration. Embedding the movement in an active current-drive readout shifts attention to the noise of the complete readout, which a design-stage estimate expresses as a few parts per million of full scale, growing as the input sensitivity increases. The example illustrates that measurement sensitivity and resolution cannot be considered independently. The treatment is aimed at master's-level students in physics with some background in statistical physics and stochastic processes, and basic familiarity with analog electronics.

papers.title: Brilliance: toward autonomous computational research in particle accelerator physics
papers.summary: Computational research in physics requires continuous interplay between simulation and scientific interpretation, demanding substantial specialist effort. Here we introduce Brilliance, a research agent that combines large language models, reusable physics knowledge and numerical simulation to conduct adaptive investigations in accelerator physics. Given a single user prompt, Brilliance designs a fourth-generation synchrotron light source that meets coupled emittance and nonlinear-acceptance requirements. Further exploration yields a design combining sub-10-pm emittance with a large dynamic aperture under realistic engineering constraints, suggesting a route towards hard-X-ray diffraction-limited operation, although the momentum-acceptance target remains unmet. Brilliance also calibrates a model of an operating light source against measured responses, accurately inferring its lattice and calibration errors. Across these studies, Brilliance autonomously revises its computational strategies in response to numerical evidence. These results demonstrate a route towards delegating sustained scientific investigations to agents equipped with domain expertise and numerical tools.

papers.title: Readout chain of SPD DAQ system
papers.summary: The Spin Physics Detector (SPD) experiment at the NICA collider of the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR) aims to study the spin structure of the nucleon and spin-related phenomena. The experimental conditions, including the high interaction rate and the large number of readout channels, require a triggerless data acquisition system with high throughput and a scalable architecture. This work presents a hardware implementation of the readout chain that extends the previously proposed SPD DAQ architecture. The chain is based on two levels of concentrators. The L1 concentrator provides the interface between the front-end electronics and the next system level and distributes synchronous signals. The L2 concentrator aggregates data streams from several L1 concentrators before transmitting them to the computing system. A key feature of the L2 implementation is the offloading of data reception, buffering, and aggregation from the host CPU to the FPGA, motivated by the large number of small packets generated by the readout electronics. The developed hardware platforms and their operating logic are presented, together with experimental results for the main interfaces and data-path components. The obtained results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed hardware architecture and its application in a scalable SPD data acquisition system.

papers.title: Thermo-viscous feedback in heat transport through fracture-matrix systems with finite thermal capacity
papers.summary: In geothermal systems, injected fluid flows along preferential fracture pathways and exchanges heat with matrix blocks. Reduced models often neglect temperature-dependent viscosity and assume unlimited matrix storage, although the thermal capacity accessible to the flow is finite. This work analyzes thermo-viscous feedback in a planar fracture-matrix system where viscosity controls discharge through the integrated hydraulic resistance, while finite capacity enters through an effective single-timescale memory fixed by initial uptake and total capacity. The reduced model gives parsimonious semi-analytical predictions with physically based parameters, verified against the nonlinear solution. A perturbation hierarchy separates matrix storage from the hydraulic response it induces, while an exponential velocity reconstruction preserves the exact terminal discharge and bounds front-moment errors within the front-moment limit model. At fixed pressure difference, heating accelerates and broadens the front, whereas cooling delays and sharpens it. The terminal discharge depends only on the endpoint viscosity ratio, while matrix uptake, storage and contrast determine its approach time. At fixed rate, viscosity alters only the pressure drop, not the thermal response. Finite thickness controls the transition to capacity-limited equilibration, and strong matrix uptake collapses the isoviscous response onto a two-variable similarity surface.

papers.title: Triadic energy routes in a short laminar separation bubble
papers.summary: The kinetic energy budget of a laminar separation bubble on a compressor blade is formed mode by mode in frequency and spanwise wavenumber from a direct numerical simulation at a Reynolds number of $2.5\times10^{5}$ based on the axial chord. The nonlinear transfer between modes is evaluated as a triadic tensor that gives the energy exchanged in every triad, the roles of its three modes, and the location of the exchange. Nine dominant tonal modes are identified: the flapping of the bubble, the Kelvin-Helmholtz mode with its sidebands, a pair of modes near reattachment, and their sum, difference, and harmonic. They hold 8% of the fluctuation energy, and their triads are responsible for 19% of the energy exchanged. Every tonal mode is fed by the mean shear and exports 69 to 82% of the energy it takes from the mean flow. The Kelvin-Helmholtz mode sends 45% of the energy it sheds to lower frequencies. The largest of these transfers is a triad in which it acts as a catalyst. The exchange in each triad is split into nine channels by velocity components. In every triad of spanwise-uniform modes, one channel dominates: the wall-tangential velocity of the donor advected by the wall-normal velocity of the catalyst. For a pair of oblique modes, the same advection by the two-dimensional Kelvin-Helmholtz mode exchanges their spanwise velocity, which the mean flow cannot produce. The rollers thus become three-dimensional through the advecting velocity of the Kelvin-Helmholtz mode, which supplies no energy to the exchange.

papers.title: Long-Baseline Phase-Coherent Microwave Reception Using Rydberg Atoms
papers.summary: A long baseline phase-coherent microwave receiver is demonstrated using a remotely interrogated cesium Rydberg atom sensor over an 8 m free-space optical link. A 3.989 GHz local oscillator (LO) is intensity-modulated onto an 852 nm optical probe and recovered remotely for atomic superheterodyne detection. A 509 nm coupling laser establishes a Rydberg electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) system addressing the 6S1/2 to 6P3/2 to 56D5/2 ladder, with microwave coupling to 57P3/2. A test signal offset by 5 kHz generates an optically detected intermediate-frequency (IF) response returned to the reference station for centralized coherent acquisition. This eliminates independent remote oscillators, electronic IF acquisition, and distributed clock synchronization. Over 10 min, the differential phase between remote and local reference exhibits a standard deviation of 0.476 deg and a minimum overlapping phase Allan deviation of 0.048 deg at approximately 200 s averaging. Following optical-link interruption, the differential phase recovers without recalibration, with a measured pre- and post-interruption difference of 0.01 deg. These results demonstrate phase coherent remotely interrogated atomic microwave reception with reduced instrumentation, supporting future distributed interferometry, multistatic radar, and coherent sensor arrays.

papers.title: Just-in-time volumetric imaging: Learning 2D-3D thoracic motion models during image-guided interventions
papers.summary: Despite two decades of innovation, cutting-edge bronchoscopic techniques still fail to yield clear diagnostic decisions in 30% of cases and miss malignancies in 20% of cases. Intraprocedural 3D imaging drastically improves both tool positioning and diagnostic yield. However, each 3D spin represents a static snapshot of an anatomy that is continuously evolving as the patient is ventilated throughout the procedure. Here, we propose just-in-time volumetric imaging, in which a patient-specific 2D--3D motion model is trained on pre-intervention scans before it is needed and then supplies volumetric images from single fluoroscopic projections during sampling. Given the inspiration-hold CBCT already acquired for navigation and an additional motion-inclusive CBCT, our optimization regime named VoxelMap-DualScan (VM-DS), solves a low-rank motion model by alternating least squares and then amortizes it into a projection encoder trained on synthesized projections with known motion, all within a 10-minute window. On eight held-out cases from the public DIR-Lab 4DCT dataset, VM-DS achieved a mean landmark target registration error of 2.8 mm, a structural similarity index of 0.95 and a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 37.7 dB. Accuracy was maintained when reducing the number of projections used for training from 227 to 23. Inference takes 1.5 ms per projection, making the framework suitable for real-time use during image-guided interventions. Code will be made available at https://github.com/Image-X-Institute/Voxelmap/tree/VM-DS

papers.title: Accelerating fits in high-energy physics and beyond
papers.summary: Data analysis in particle physics often involves optimizing a loss function that quantifies how well a theoretical model describes the observed data, in order to estimate the parameters of the model. This is referred to as fitting. As datasets grow larger and more expensive analysis methods are used, the time required to perform this parameter estimation can be a limiting factor. This work explores techniques for accelerating the fitting process, and measures their performance on a set of models representative of a variety of physics fits. We compare the speed and precision of variants of well-known optimization algorithms, namely Newton's method, BFGS, and the Migrad algorithm (commonly used in particle physics fits). We observe significant speedups when using some algorithms: most notably, some variants of BFGS are about ten times faster than Migrad, while achieving the same precision. For quasi-Newtonian algorithms like BFGS and Migrad, we find that the initial value of the Hessian matrix has a large impact on the runtime. We additionally discuss methods for accelerating the evaluation of the loss function and its derivatives, using algebraic simplifications, automatic differentiation, and modern hardware features. We explore techniques for achieving good precision with 32-bit operations, which can achieve significantly higher throughput on the GPU. Lastly we explore efficient parallelization strategies for the CPU and GPU. All of the techniques and algorithms in this paper are implemented in our new FastFit library, which was used for all of our benchmarks.

papers.title: Theoretical study of high-order harmonic generation in solids based on deep-learning methods
papers.summary: High-order harmonic generation (HHG) in solids provides a compact and coherent EUV radiation, which has attracted considerable attention. Many theoretical methods for laser-crystal interactions are developed. However, an approach to treat large-scale amorphous systems with ab-initio accuracy is still lacking because of the enormous computational cost. Here, we incorporate molecular dynamics and tight-binding electron Hamiltonians based on deep-learning methods to solve the problem efficiently. Its accuracy is validated by comparing the HHG spectra of monolayer hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) with those obtained using existing methods. Then we use it to study the temperature-dependent HHG in bulk Si. We uncover a distinct harmonic-order-dependent thermal response: low-order harmonics are enhanced with increasing temperature, whereas high-order harmonics are suppressed. The former is caused by the modification of the inter-site hopping in the system, while the latter is mainly influenced by the structural disorder induced by the thermal effects, in agreement with experimental observations. This work establishes a scalable computational strategy for investigating HHG in solids and provides new insights into the interplay between lattice fluctuations and ultrafast electron dynamics.

papers.title: Attenuation of shoaling extreme wave crests by artificial salt marshes
papers.summary: Laboratory experiments in a wave flume investigated the attenuation of shoaling extreme waves by artificial salt marshes placed immediately before an abrupt depth transition. Increasing vegetation density systematically reduced the excess kurtosis of the surface elevation distribution in the intermediate water depth regime. Nonetheless, attenuation exhibits a short saturation regime at low vegetation densities, whereas at very high densities, excess kurtosis decreases significantly across the gauges. However, kurtosis attenuation becomes ineffective as waves approach shallow-water conditions or as second-order nonlinear effects become significant. Furthermore, the highest experimental densities where the kurtosis is tamed exceed typical natural salt marsh stem densities. Thus, in natural settings, salt marshes are likely to provide only partial mitigation of extreme wave statistics in intermediate and shallow water depths, as the wave field retains some hazardous nonlinearity.

papers.title: On-ground calibration of the X-ray, gamma-ray, and relativistic electron detector onboard TARANIS
papers.summary: We developed the X-ray, Gamma-ray and Relativistic Electron detector (XGRE) onboard the TARANIS satellite, to investigate high-energy phenomena associated with lightning discharges such as terrestrial gamma-ray flashes and terrestrial electron beams. XGRE consisted of three sensors. Each sensor has one layer of LaBr$_{3}$ crystals for X-ray/gamma-ray detections, and two layers of plastic scintillators for electron and charged-particle discrimination. Since 2018, the flight model of XGRE was developed, and validation and calibration tests, such as a thermal cycle test and a calibration test with the sensors onboard the satellite were performed before the launch of TARANIS on 17 November 2020. The energy range of the LaBr$_{3}$ crystals sensitive to X-rays and gamma rays was determined to be 0.04-11.6 MeV, 0.08-11.0 MeV, and 0.08-11.3 MeV for XGRE1, 2, and 3, respectively. The energy resolution at 0.662 MeV (full width at half maximum) was to be 20.5%, 25.9%, and 28.6%, respectively. Results from the calibration test were then used to validate a simulation model of XGRE and TARANIS. By performing Monte Carlo simulations with the verified model, we calculated effective areas of XGRE to X-rays, gamma rays, electrons, and detector responses to incident photons and electrons coming from various elevation and azimuth angles.

papers.title: Computational quantum transport: a scattering approach perspective
papers.summary: This review is devoted to the different techniques that have been developed to compute the phase-coherent transport properties of quantum nanoelectronic systems connected to electrodes. Beside a review of the different algorithms proposed in the literature, we provide a comprehensive and pedagogical derivation of the two formalisms on which these techniques are based: the scattering approach and the (nonequilibrium) Green's function approach. We show that the scattering problem can be formulated as a system of linear equations and that different existing algorithms for solving this scattering problem amount to different sequences of Gaussian elimination. We explicitly prove the equivalence of the two formalisms. We discuss the stability and numerical complexity of the existing methods. The review ends with a selection of a few applications where numerical calculations were instrumental in shaping our understanding of the physics.

papers.title: Active morphodynamics of intracellular organelles in the trafficking pathway
papers.summary: From the Golgi apparatus to endosomes, organelles in the endomembrane system exhibit complex and varied morphologies that are often related to their function. These membrane-bound organelles operate far from equilibrium due to directed fluxes of trafficking vesicles, yet the physical principles governing the emergence and maintenance of these morphologies remain elusive. By coarse-graining the active mechanochemical cycles associated with individual fission and fusion events, we show how vesicular trafficking manifests at the hydrodynamic scale, generating not only fluxes of membrane area and encapsulated volume but also active stresses that mediate momentum transfer between an organelle and its cytosolic environment. The fluid and deformable nature of the bounding membrane gives rise to novel physics by coupling these nonequilibrium forces to organelle composition, morphology, and hydrodynamic flows. We demonstrate how both stable compartment drift and ramified sac-like morphologies, reminiscent of Golgi cisternal motion and shape, emerge from the same nonequilibrium dynamics of fission and fusion.

papers.title: LightPFP: A Lightweight Route to Ab Initio Accuracy at Scale
papers.summary: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) bridge the gap between quantum-mechanical accuracy and scalable molecular simulations. However, a fundamental trade-off persists: universal MLIPs (u-MLIPs) offer broad transferability but are computationally expensive, whereas task-specific MLIPs (ts-MLIPs) achieve high efficiency at the expense of costly DFT training data. Here we introduce LightPFP, a data-efficient knowledge distillation framework. Instead of relying on expensive DFT calculations, LightPFP constructs a distilled ts-MLIP by using a u-MLIP to generate high-quality, material-specific training data, while employing a pre-trained lightweight model to further improve data efficiency. Across diverse material systems, LightPFP reduces model development time by approximately three orders of magnitude compared with DFT-based workflows, while maintaining DFT-level accuracy. Combined with a LAMMPS/Kokkos inference backend, LightPFP achieves more than three orders of magnitude higher inference efficiency than u-MLIP baselines while enabling simulations of systems thousands of times larger. When the teacher exhibits systematic bias, LightPFP supports few-shot precision correction using as few as 10 high-accuracy DFT configurations, as demonstrated by reproducing MgO's experimental melting point. This u-MLIP-driven distillation establishes a scalable route to high-fidelity, data-efficient MLIPs, accelerating the pace of materials discovery and design.

papers.title: Quantum Orthogonal Separable Physics-Informed Neural Networks
papers.summary: We introduce Quantum Orthogonal Separable Physics-Informed Neural Networks (QO-SPINNs), which replace selected dense hidden transformations in physics-informed PDE models with quantum-compatible orthogonal maps. A pyramidal reconfigurable-beamsplitter circuit realizes these maps with $\Theta(d)$ circuit depth. Under the stated signed-readout access model and fixed per-call failure probability, a width-$d$ map has sequential access-cost upper bound $\mathcal O(d\log d/\epsilon^2)$, which is asymptotically smaller than the $\Theta(d^2)$ cost of conventional direct dense multiplication when $\epsilon(d)^{-2}\log d=o(d)$. Because unary state preparation discards magnitude, we retain each hidden-state norm classically and restore it after readout, yielding the exact map $Wh$ under ideal readout. We study this construction in two complementary settings: forward PDE regression and a norm-controlled residual model for representation geometry and uncertainty quantification. In the norm-controlled model, structural orthogonality yields explicit bi-Lipschitz bounds, while finite-readout analysis relates sufficient reconstruction precision to a prescribed physical-coordinate resolution through trained-model constants. This makes the access-cost condition assessable for trained checkpoints, although favorable fixed-resolution scaling across widths is not established. A post-hoc Bayesian-linear covariance provides uncertainty from the same frozen predictor, and cross-PDE transfer shows that strong distance-awareness can persist even when absolute coverage calibration fails. All Quantum Orthogonal (QO) layers are evaluated by classical simulation: the results therefore characterize a quantum-compatible structured neural primitive rather than demonstrating a practical quantum-hardware advantage.

papers.title: A quantitative Hohenberg-Kohn theorem and the unexpected regularity of density functional theory in one spatial dimension
papers.summary: In this paper we investigate the (Kohn-Sham) density-to-potential map in the case of spinless fermions in one spatial dimension, whose existence has been rigorously established by the first author in [Lett. Math. Phys. 116, (2026), no. 27. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11005-026-02051-1]. Here, we focus on the regularity of this map as a function of the density and the coupling constant in front of the interaction term. More precisely, we first prove a quantitative version of the Hohenberg-Kohn theorem, thereby showing that this map is Lipschitz continuous with respect to the natural Sobolev norms in the space of densities and potentials. In particular, this implies that the inverse (Kohn-Sham) problem is not only well-posed but also Lipschitz stable. Using this result, we then show that the density-to-potential map is in fact real analytic with respect to both the density and the interaction strength. As a consequence, we obtain a holomorphic extension of the universal constrained-search functional to a suitable subset of complex-valued densities. This partially extends the DFT framework to non-self-adjoint Schr\"odinger operators. As further applications of these results, we also establish the existence of an exchange-only part of the exchange-correlation potential, and justify the G\"orling-Levy perturbation expansion for the correlation energy.

papers.title: Gauge-Invariant Phase Mapping to Intensity Lobes of Structured Light via Closed-Loop Atomic Dark States
papers.summary: We present an analytical model showing how the gauge-invariant loop phase in a three-level closed-loop atomic system imprints as bright-dark lobes in Laguerre Gaussian probe beam intensity patterns. In the weak probe limit, the output intensity in such systems include Beer-Lambert absorption, a scattering term and loop phase dependent interference term with optical depth controlling visibility. These systems enable mapping of arbitrary phases via interference rotation and offer a platform to measure Berry phase. Berry phase emerge as a geometric holonomy acquired by the dark states during adiabatic traversal of LG phase defined in a toroidal parameter space. Manifesting as fringe shifts which are absent in open systems, experimental realization using cold atoms or solid state platforms appears feasible, positioning structured light in closed-loop systems as ideal testbeds for geometric phases in quantum optics.

papers.title: Global Well-Posedness of the Vacuum Free Boundary Problem for the Degenerate Compressible Navier-Stokes Equations With Large Data of Spherical Symmetry
papers.summary: The study of global-in-time dynamics of vacuum is crucial for understanding viscous flows. In particular, physical vacuum, which ensures a finite, nontrivial pressure-induced acceleration in the normal direction on the moving boundary, naturally arises in the motion of gaseous stars and shallow water. The corresponding large-data problems for spherically symmetric flows remain open, due to the combined difficulties of coordinate singularity at the origin and degeneracy on the moving boundary. In this paper, we analyze the free boundary problem for the barotropic compressible Navier-Stokes equations with density-dependent viscosity coefficients (as in the shallow water equations) in two and three spatial dimensions. For a general class of spherically symmetric initial densities: $\rho_0^{\beta}\in H^3$ with $\beta\in (\frac{1}{3},\gamma-1]$ ($\gamma$: adiabatic exponent), vanishing on the moving boundary in the form of a distance function, we establish the global existence of the unique classical solution with large data. Moreover, our solution is classical up to the moving boundary, and the physical vacuum is allowed for the data under consideration here when $\beta=\gamma-1$. The key ingredient of our analysis is to obtain the uniform control over the first-order spatial derivatives of the flow map $\eta(t,r)$ in spherically symmetric Lagrangian coordinates, which is achieved by some novel density-weighted estimates and flow-map-weighted estimates for the solutions.

papers.title: Gravitational wave detection via photon-graviton scattering and quantum interference
papers.summary: We present a fully quantum field-theoretic framework for gravitational wave (GW) detection, describing the interaction as inelastic photon-graviton scattering. We demonstrate that for \textit{a coherent graviton state}, this microscopic model explicitly reproduces the standard classical geometric-optics time delay, providing a rigorous consistency test of the correspondence limit. We propose a detection scheme based on Hong-Ou-Mandel interference, where the GW-induced spectral shifts render entangled photon pairs distinguishable. This encodes the gravitational signal into the modulation of photon coincidence rates --- a quantum observable robust against laser intensity noise. Furthermore, we show that non-classical graviton states, such as squeezed states, induce unique decoherence signatures, establishing theoretical bounds on gravitational decoherence and defining the operational limits for probing the quantum nature of gravity.

papers.title: Decoherence-Induced Multiphoton Interference
papers.summary: Decoherence is usually deemed detrimental to quantum information processing. Its control and minimization require significant costs and operating overheads, constituting a major hurdle to the practical deployment of quantum technologies. Yet, quantum mechanics provides for counterintuitive, sometimes surprisingly useful, phenomena and effects associated with decoherence, leading to unusual practical utilities. Here we demonstrate such an example of fundamental interest and practical potential, where quantum interference is created among multiple photons through their dissipative coupling to a shared reservoir. On a thin-film lithium niobate chip, we dissipatively link two spontaneous parametric down-converters through a common, highly lossy channel to create phase-sensitive multiphoton states. Our results show that faithful correlations can be established among two, three, and four photons, and tuned by shifting the relative phase between the driving pumps for the converters. This experiment highlights an under-explored territory in quantum science and technology, where loss and decoherence serve as resources, rather than adversaries, for quantum information processing.

papers.title: Dynamic Behaviors of Materials Under Angle-Resolved Experiments: A Matrix Framework for Nonlinear Physics
papers.summary: Matter and external stimuli interact dynamically almost everywhere in nature. Under an applied field, a material seldom stays in the state in which it was characterized, and its properties change with time. Angle-resolved experiments are the standard way to resolve direction-dependent properties, however, current theoretical tools for data analysis are built for static states, leaving dynamic behaviors largely neglected. Here, we develop a generalized ``input-coefficient-output'' (ICO) approach that constructs spatial operation matrices and symmetry-reduced coefficient matrices across diverse physical systems, as we verify for nonlinear optics, elasticity, electrostriction and magnetostriction, and a Python program is released for convenient application. Using angle-resolved polarized second-harmonic generation (SHG) as an example, we focus on the dynamic modeling of material properties under angle-dependent stimuli, construct dynamic matrix equations that capture the time-dependent evolution of material responses, and propose three dynamic models and a point-to-point data fitting method. For the SHG experiments performed on $T_d-$WTe$_2$, the discrete dynamic model captures the asymmetric characteristics of the measured polar pattern with a significantly improved coefficient of determination ($R^2$ increasing from 0.567 to 0.773), whereas conventional static models are constrained to a symmetric curve. The evolution operator extracted from the dynamic model connects the macroscopic measurement to microscopic intermediate states during their interaction with stimuli. This work provides a practical matrix framework for dynamic modeling of material properties, paving the way for exploring complex nonlinear physics under realistic experimental conditions.

papers.title: Ultrastrong Coupling Signatures in Photon Statistics from Terahertz Higgs-Polaritons
papers.summary: The ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity photons and quantum materials has emerged as a pathway to modify materials properties, however definitive signatures of ultrastrong coupling remain elusive. Focusing on the quantum photon statistics of light transmitted through a cavity-embedded superconductor, we show that a two-photon Higgs polariton at strong coupling realizes a photonic nonlinearity at the single terahertz photon level. We find that as light-matter coupling increases, the photon statistics show pronounced changes due to the formation of a hybrid photon-matter dark-cavity state with finite photon occupancy, producing testable signatures of ultrastrong coupling. We derive a non-Markovian input output relation and study the cavity-embedded superconductor 2H-NbSe2 as it approaches ultrastrong light-matter coupling. Our results reveal a diagnostic for ultrastrong coupling in the two-photon coincidence statistics that is absent in total counts.

papers.title: Solvent-induced memory effects in a model electrolyte
papers.summary: The fluctuations of ions in polar solvents remain poorly understood theoretically due to the complex coupling between ionic motion and solvent polarization. Indeed, while all-atom resolution can be achieved in numerical simulations, analytical approaches require suitable levels of coarse-graining. In this work, we describe ions and solvent molecules as interacting Brownian particles and use stochastic density functional theory to derive a generalized Langevin equation for the ionic charge density, explicitly accounting for solvent-mediated memory effects. In the regime where there is a clear timescale separation between fast solvent and slow ion dynamics, we obtain simple expressions for dynamical charge structure factors, which are validated by BD simulations. For slow solvents, we predict an emerging two-step relaxation in ionic dynamics. These results provide a mesoscopic approach for ion-solvent dynamics and open pathways to study fluctuation-induced phenomena in electrolytes.

papers.title: A first-principles approach for predicting infrared optical properties of solids
papers.summary: We present a simplified formalism for predicting infrared optical constants from first-principles calculations. Addressing limitations of the widely used four-parameter semi-quantum Lorentz model, the proposed approach bridges the gap between the harmonic three-parameter model and full self-energy-based methods. By incorporating essential anharmonic effects including four-phonon scattering and phonon renormalisation, the model provides an efficient and accurate alternative while maintaining low computational cost. The frequency-dependent refractive indices of MgO and rutile TiO$_2$ are computed and compared with experimental data, demonstrating good quantitative agreement. The framework offers a practical approach for predicting optical properties of materials across a wide range of materials.

papers.title: Tailoring the properties of YBa$_{2}$Cu$_{3}$O$_{7-\delta}$ thin films by 30-keV He$^+$ irradiation: An enabling route to superconducting device nanopatterning
papers.summary: Focused helium ion beam (He-FIB) irradiation with 30-keV ions is a key tool for nanoscale patterning and defect engineering in high transition temperature (Tc) cuprate superconducting devices, yet its usable fluence window is constrained by the competing requirements of reliable superconductivity suppression and minimal structural degradation. In this work, we provide a comprehensive dataset on the effects of large-area 30-keV He+ ion exposure on the electric transport and superconducting properties of epitaxial YBa2Cu3O7 (YBCO) thin films. X-ray diffraction shows a fluence-driven loss of crystalline order accompanied by an out-of-plane lattice expansion and an orthorhombic-to-tetragonal transition, culminating in predominant amorphization at the highest fluence of 1 x 10^16 cm^-2. Raman spectra exhibit increasing disorder while lacking signatures of oxygen depletion, indicating that irradiation mainly generates oxygen-related Frenkel defects rather than changing the carrier concentration. Consistently, with increasing fluence, the normal-state resistivity \rho_N(T) at temperature T above Tc increases strongly, while d \rho_N/d T remains nearly unchanged at moderate fluence. The suppression of Tc is accurately described by Abrikosov-Gor'kov pair breaking and reaches complete quenching of superconductivity at 4.5 x 10^15 cm^-2. The anisotropic upper critical fields decrease approximately exponentially with increasing fluence, the vortex activation energy is reduced, and the anisotropy drops, in contrast to oxygen-depleted YBCO. Hall-angle analysis confirms a nearly constant carrier density but a systematic increase in defect scattering and reduced mobility, consistent with a crossover toward the dirty limit at high fluence. These results establish quantitative fluence thresholds and a practical operational window for He-FIB nanopatterning of YBCO quantum circuits.

papers.title: Connecting Quantum Tomography and Quantum Retrodiction
papers.summary: Quantum tomography and quantum retrodiction are traditionally viewed as separate inference tasks. We show that the two are manifestations of the same underlying principle. We prove that the Petz recovery map of a measurement channel is a gradient of the log-likelihood used in maximum-likelihood tomography, and we derive its extension to arbitrary quantum channels. Consequently, for measurement channels, repeated applications of the Petz map monotonically increase the likelihood, naturally yielding a method for quantum tomography.

papers.title: Discovery of connectivity-trainability trade-off of IQP circuits for Hamiltonian optimization
papers.summary: Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial-time (IQP) circuits are promising candidates for near-term quantum computing due to the conjectured classical hardness of their sampling task and their shallow, highly parallelizable structure. Despite extensive studies of their complexity-theoretic properties, the role of circuit connectivity in their trainability as variational ansatze remains poorly understood. In this work, we present an investigation of IQP circuits for Hamiltonian optimization that traces a mechanistic chain linking circuit connectivity, entanglement generation, and gradient scaling: increasing connectivity drives the circuit output toward Haar-like statistics and volume-law entanglement, and this increase in entanglement is consistently associated with an exponential decay of the gradient variance and degraded optimization performance, while sparser architectures retain stable gradients at the cost of global expressibility and entanglement capacity. This connectivity-entanglement-gradient mechanism produces a nontrivial connectivity-trainability trade-off, demonstrating that effective IQP-based Hamiltonian optimization requires a balance between global expressibility and trainability rather than maximal expressivity alone. In particular, on our benchmarks, a circuit generating no entanglement already matches the optimization performance of more highly connected circuits, and a circular topology retains entanglement capacity while preserving trainability, making it a broadly effective choice among the architectures considered.

papers.title: Efficient Large-Scale STEM-EELS Simulations With Torched-TACAW
papers.summary: The time auto-correlation of auxiliary wave functions (TACAW) method enables efficient simulations of ultra-low-loss electron energy loss spectra (EELS) arising from vibrational and magnon excitations. In practical applications to realistic materials systems, however, TACAW calculations become challenging due to the large system sizes required for models containing defects, interfaces, impurities, or grain boundaries, as well as the substantial computational cost and data throughput associated with molecular dynamics and multislice calculations. Here we discuss a practical methodology for large-scale TACAW simulations and present torched-TACAW, a freely available implementation of the TACAW part of the described workflow for efficient STEM-EELS simulations. The overall approach combines molecular dynamics based on foundational machine-learned interatomic potentials, partitioning of elongated supercells, and on-the-fly processing of multislice outputs in order to enable near ab initio quality simulations with tractable memory use and data flow. Using rutile TiO2 as a model system, we analyze important numerical aspects of the method, including windowing and supercell partitioning, and demonstrate atomic-resolution STEM-EELS simulations for thick samples.

papers.title: Broadband characterization of polarization mode dispersion for quantum communication channels
papers.summary: We present a method for characterizing depolarization in fiber channels carrying broadband polarization-encoded optical signals. Wavelength-dependent polarization mode dispersion maps each input polarization to a trajectory on the Poincar\'e sphere; we show that the singular value decomposition of the band-averaged rotation matrix yields, in closed form, the optimal input states, the associated mutually unbiased measurement bases, and the resulting projection error probabilities. The three singular values provide a compact, bandwidth-dependent channel signature that distinguishes first- from higher-order dispersion, and yield the bandwidth at which the worst-case error probability reaches 3% as a practical filtering budget. We perform a second-order analysis of the band average that treats the two higher-order mechanisms: variation of the differential group delay at a fixed principal-state axis and wander of that axis with wavelength. We characterize 12 deployed fiber links in Masdar City and demonstrate mitigation by concatenating two channels through a single polarization controller, a step towards nonlocal compensation. The analysis is implemented in an openly available Python library for fiber-channel characterization.

papers.title: Steering the dynamics by controlling the temporal interaction network
papers.summary: Many real-world coupled dynamical systems have their interaction structure and strength that evolve or adapt over time. Here, we investigate how one can control the state of a system by tuning its temporal interaction network. We present a framework based on nonlinear optimal control, where one has control over the time-dependent coupling matrix of a dynamical system. We show how to obtain the gradient of the Lagrangian functional of a generic optimal control problem using the adjoint method, where the control variables are multiplicative inputs. We illustrate the theory with the precision cost that aims at steering the nodal states to prescribed target trajectories. We first focus on a linear time-variant system for which further expressions of the gradient can be obtained. Second, we uncover the temporal interaction that pushes a nonlinear neural units model towards target trajectories. For both systems, we numerically solve the optimal control problem, imposing various constraint on the structure of the controlled edges. The workflow presented here can be leveraged to steer the dynamics of systems with artificial or engineered interaction that is tunable.

papers.title: Hybrid Dynamical Simulation Reveals Apparent Stiffening of Flexible Protein Lattices Driving Membrane Bending
papers.summary: Membrane-deforming protein lattices play a central role in essential and pathogenic remodeling processes, including clathrin-mediated endocytosis and viral budding. Simulating these systems at biologically relevant length and time scales requires mesoscale approaches that preserve structural detail. We present a hybrid simulation framework that couples a particle-based flexible protein lattice to a continuum membrane model, enabling systematic investigation of how lattice geometry and rigidity influence membrane remodeling. We validate the coupled model by comparing simulation results with theoretical predictions for membranes under increasing tension. Using buckling-based deformations of pre-assembled clathrin lattices, we quantify the lattice flexural rigidity and establish a direct relationship between the force constants in the coarse-grained energy function and the emergent lattice mechanics. We then compare this flexural rigidity, $\kappa_{l,\mathrm{flex}}$, to an effective rigidity, $\kappa_{l,\mathrm{eff}}$, commonly used in continuum descriptions of sphere-forming protein assemblies. Although $\kappa_{l,\mathrm{flex}}$ is set solely by the energy function, $\kappa_{l,\mathrm{eff}}$ depends on lattice size and connectivity, with the two measures converging for weakly-connected lattices. As a result, with lattice growth, the effective rigidity relevant for spherical bud formation increases and the relaxation timescale decreases. This size-dependent stiffening highlights the importance of structural details in interpreting lattice mechanics and cautions against assuming a single constant stiffness. We demonstrate the generality of the method by applying it to pre-assembled viral lattices generated with reaction-diffusion simulations. This work provides a validated framework for simulating deformable protein assemblies of diverse geometry coupled to membrane dynamics and remodeling.

papers.title: Emergent topological structure in spontaneous brain-organoid activity
papers.summary: Neural activity is widely held to organize on low-dimensional structure embedded in a high-dimensional state space. Persistent homology reads such structure directly from the pattern of pairwise correlations, without assuming in advance which variables are relevant. We apply persistent homology to microelectrode-array (MEA) recordings of spontaneous activity from human (Lancaster) and mouse (Pasca) cortical organoids, spanning 25-197 sorted units, and ask whether topological data analysis resolves structure at the node counts that neural recordings actually deliver. Building weighted networks in correlation space and characterizing them by Vietoris-Rips filtration, we find that the first homology (H1, loops) rises significantly above a rate- and population-preserving null in 14 of 18 datasets, all of which remain significant after correction for testing 18 datasets. Random removal of neural units leaves the loops largely intact. Removing the units that form the loops disrupts them more than removing equally connected units does. Topological richness grows with network size, and second homology (H2) exceeds the null only in the larger networks. These results show that persistent homology resolves structured topology in neural recordings at the scale experiments actually deliver.

papers.title: Norm of resonance states in quantum scattering and electromagnetic systems
papers.summary: Resonance states spatially diverge and are thus not square integrable. Instead, their norm is defined by the biorthogonal scalar product of left and right states. We replace the corresponding volume integral over infinite space by a convenient boundary integral in piecewise-homogeneous systems and apply this procedure to diverse physical settings. For a quantum particle in any number of dimensions we treat hard-wall and piecewise-constant potentials. For electromagnetic systems with piecewise-homogeneous material properties, we consider three-dimensional and effectively two-dimensional cavities.

papers.title: Spectral properties of mesoscale fluctuations in interplanetary coronal mass ejections
papers.summary: Magnetic fields in interplanetary coronal mass ejections (ICMEs) often display a flux rope structure at large scales and a turbulent cascade of fluctuations at smaller scales. However, the nature of fluctuations at transition scales between the flux rope and turbulence - i.e., at mesoscales - has not been previously examined in detail. Mesoscale fluctuations of the magnetic field in 142 ICME intervals with clear flux rope signatures at 1 au have been examined using wavelet power spectra, with "mesoscale" defined here as spacecraft-frame frequencies $10^{-4}\ \text{Hz}<f_\mathrm{sc}< 10^{-3}\ \text{Hz}$, equivalent to timescales $2.8\ \text{hr}\gtrsim \tau \gtrsim 17\ \text{min}$. The spectra were found to be significantly less steep at mesoscales than at larger and smaller scales, with an average spectral slope close to $-1$ at these intermediate scales. The mesoscale fluctuations had relatively high cross helicity magnitudes and low compressibility, suggesting a significant degree of Alfv\'enicity, while also having more negative residual energy than the turbulent fluctuations found at smaller scales. Uncertainties in the spectral slope values at mesoscales were used to distinguish between spectra showing a relatively smooth power-law behavior or (less commonly) a more bumpy trend; the smoother power-law intervals had a balanced cross helicity distribution while the more bumpy spectra had a predominantly antisunward cross helicity. Slow wind intervals were similarly analyzed, and showed similar properties to the ICMEs. These results indicate that a spectrally narrow $1/f$ range is typically present in ICMEs at mesoscales.

papers.title: Time-Reversal-Invariant Altermagnetic Acoustic Crystals
papers.summary: Altermagnets have emerged as a new class of magnetic materials that combine spin-split electronic bands with zero net magnetization. Extending this paradigm to classical-wave systems has, however, been fundamentally challenging because conventional realizations require broken time-reversal symmetry (TRS). Here, we overcome this limitation by introducing a pseudospin degree of freedom and constructing a pseudo-time-reversal operator that faithfully reproduces the action of its physical counterpart while preserving actual TRS. Building on this framework, we theoretically propose and experimentally realize the first time-reversal-invariant altermagnetic acoustic crystal. Acoustic measurements directly reveal pseudospin-dependent band splitting--a defining hallmark of altermagnetism--under strictly TRS-preserving conditions. Moreover, the altermagnetic acoustic crystal exhibits sublattice-pseudospin locking, enabling flexible control over acoustic pseudospin splitting and filtering. Our work establishes acoustic crystals as a versatile platform for exploring altermagnetic physics and opens new avenues for spin-inspired wave manipulation in nonmagnetic devices.

papers.title: Machine-learned exchange-correlation functionals for molecules, solids, and reactive surfaces
papers.summary: The application of density functional theory to heterogeneous catalysis is hindered by the shortcomings of conventional density functional approximations. We combine machine learning with explicitly non-local physically informed descriptors and introduce an exchange-correlation functional (CIDER26SS) framework regularized for wide transferability. CIDER26SS is size-extensive, highly efficient, provides a balanced and accurate description of both molecular and solid-state systems, and is specifically well-optimized for transition metal surface chemistry. Surpassing existing conventional functionals, CIDER26SS resolves the CO/Pt puzzle, identifying the correct binding site for CO adsorption on the Pt(111) surface, along with an accurate adsorption energy, Pt lattice constant, and surface energy. Predictions agree well with the experimental values, even when all bulk and surface data for Pt are excluded from the training set. Remarkably, CIDER26SS exceeds the accuracy of semilocal approximations even for systems far outside the training domain.

papers.title: Decay versus dephasing in Rydberg analog optimization: the exchange rate depends on the readout
papers.summary: Numerical studies of noisy Rydberg-atom optimization compress decoherence into a single rate, treating spontaneous decay ($\Gamma$) and dephasing ($\gamma$) as equivalent. We resolve the two as independent Lindblad axes for quantum annealing of unit-disk maximum independent set at fixed annealing time and ask how their relative effect depends on the readout. For the raw readout the size error collapses onto the effective dephasing rate $u=\kappa\Gamma+\gamma$, and at small noise a unit of decay rate degrades the result as much as $\kappa=7.4$ units of dephasing rate; a collapse fit across the whole grid returns 8.3. After greedy completion followed by a $(1,2)$-swap local search, classical post-processing of polynomial cost, the exchange rate falls to $\kappa=1.6$, and at the calibrated operating point of a commercial device dephasing produces three quarters of the noise-induced error instead of two fifths. First-order perturbation theory built from noiseless propagation gives the decay and dephasing susceptibilities of every readout, raw or post-processed, to a few parts in $10^6$ of the full Lindblad result. The raw asymmetry is set at the end of the schedule, where a decay event deletes an atom and a dephasing event leaves the readout unchanged. Post-processing refills most deletions and leaves misplaced atoms, which the two channels produce at comparable rates. Which channel limits a device therefore depends on the readout as well as on the hardware.

papers.title: Liquid crystalline order and its impact on shape evolution of fluid lipid membranes
papers.summary: We consider extensions of the classical curvature-elasticity free energy for a fluid lipid membrane, explicitly treating the liquid crystal structure of the membrane, which results from the lipid molecules that are, on average, oriented normal to the surface. Locally varying liquid crystal order leads to local variations in bending rigidities and surface viscosity and thus influences the shape evolution. This provides a multiscale coupling between the local membrane mechanics on the level of the lipids and the mesoscopic length and time scales of biological functions. Numerical simulations in the one-constant approximation demonstrate the impact of local membrane mechanics on the emerging equilibrium shapes. These shapes not only depend on the specified conserved surface area and enclosed volume, as for the classical curvature-elasticity free energy, but also the elastic parameter and are characterized by a reduced liquid crystal order at highly curved regions. The modified shapes and their varying liquid crystal order, as function of curvature, provide experimentally testable properties. Exploring the dynamic evolution demonstrate a tight coupling of tangential flow, shape evolution and liquid crystalline order. We further point to model extensions towards lipid phase separation and asymmetric lipid bilayers and biological implications.
